skills.title: Anchoring & Adjustment
skills.subtitle: How the first number you hear hijacks every number after it
skills.challenge: This week, before any negotiation or purchase, write down your target number BEFORE hearing their opening. Track how many times the first number you heard pulled your final number toward it.
skills.definition: Anchoring and adjustment is a heuristic where people make numerical estimates by starting from an initial value (the anchor) and adjusting from it to reach a final answer. The critical finding: adjustments are almost always insufficient, so the final estimate is biased toward the anchor. Even completely random anchors massively influence estimates.
skills.content:
## Definition

Anchoring and adjustment is a heuristic where people make numerical estimates by **starting from an initial value (the "anchor") and adjusting** from it to reach a final answer. The critical finding: adjustments are almost always **insufficient**, so the final estimate is biased toward the anchor.

## Key Findings

- A **completely random anchor** (a spin of a wheel of fortune) massively influenced estimates of the percentage of African countries in the UN. Subjects anchored at 10 gave a median estimate of 25; those anchored at 65 gave 45. (summary-1-01-judgment-under-uncertainty)
- Incentives for accuracy did not eliminate the effect
- **Conjunctive events are overestimated:** People overestimate the probability that ALL of a series of likely events will occur (product of probabilities < individual probabilities). This leads to overoptimistic project plans.
- **Disjunctive events are underestimated:** People underestimate the probability that AT LEAST ONE of a series of unlikely events will occur. This leads to underestimation of risk in complex systems.
- **overconfidence-in-calibration:** People set far too narrow confidence intervals. When asked for 98% confidence ranges, the true value fell outside ~30% of the time — a 15x error rate.

## Mechanisms

Anchoring works through two potential pathways (the 1974 paper does not distinguish them, but later research does):

1. **Insufficient adjustment:** People start from the anchor and serially adjust until they reach a plausible value — then stop too soon. The adjustment is effortful and terminates prematurely.
2. **Selective accessibility (proposed in later research):** The anchor makes anchor-consistent information more accessible in memory, biasing the judgment toward the anchor without any conscious "adjustment" process.

The conjunctive/disjunctive bias arises because people anchor on the probability of individual events and insufficiently adjust for the compounding effect of combining many events.

## Applications

- **Negotiation:** First offers serve as anchors. The party who sets the initial number has a powerful advantage — all subsequent discussion adjusts from that point. (Critical for Phase 5 — getting-to-yes, negotiation-genius, never-split-the-difference)
- **Pricing:** Initial prices anchor perceived value. A $100 product marked down to $60 is perceived differently than the same product always priced at $60.
- **Project planning:** The tendency to overestimate conjunctive probabilities = systematic overoptimism about project timelines (the "planning fallacy")
- **Risk assessment:** The tendency to underestimate disjunctive probabilities = systematic underestimation of system failure rates
- **Salary negotiation:** The first number spoken anchors the range. Even knowing about anchoring doesn't fully immunize against it.

## Cross-References
- **Related concepts:** representativeness, availability, overconfidence-in-calibration
- **Key authors:** tversky, kahneman
- **Frameworks that use this:** heuristics-and-biases-program

## Bazerman & Moore Extensions

Bazerman and Moore (summary-2-08-bazerman-ch3) significantly extend the anchoring research with additional studies and mechanisms:

- **Two distinct mechanisms (Epley, 2004):** (1) When an anchor is externally set, it leads to a biased search for anchor-consistent information (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999, 2000, 2001). E.g., a house with a high list price leads you to notice positive features. (2) When someone develops their own anchor, they start from it and insufficiently adjust (Epley & Gilovich, 2001). E.g., estimating when George Washington was elected by adjusting from 1776
- **Paying for accuracy does not reduce anchoring** -- unlike many biases, incentives fail to eliminate the effect
- **Mussweiler and Strack (2000):** Participants anchored on high vs. low car prices were faster at recognizing words associated with expensive vs. cheap cars -- the anchor primes related concepts
- **Extreme price anchors:** Simply exposing someone to an extreme price increases willingness to pay for a product, even if the product is in a different category (Janiszewski, Lichtenstein, & Belyavsky, 2008; Adaval & Wyer, 2011)
- **Arbitrary action anchors:** Participants asked to draw long lines gave higher estimates of the Mississippi River's length than those who drew short lines (Oppenheimer, LeBoeuf, & Brewer, 2008)
- **Professional auditors:** Joyce and Biddle (1981) showed anchoring among practicing Big Four auditors -- fraud incidence estimates were 16.52 vs. 43.11 per 1000 depending on the arbitrary anchor in the question
- **Judicial sentencing:** Judges' sentences are influenced by anchors as irrelevant as a roll of dice (Englich & Mussweiler, 2001; Englich, Mussweiler, & Strack, 2006)
- **Education:** Children tracked by ability at an early age become anchored to expectations; Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968) showed teacher expectations (anchors) influence actual student performance
- **Race as anchor:** Duncan (1976) found the same behavior perceived as more aggressive when exhibited by an African American than a European American -- race serves as an anchor for behavioral expectations
- **Salary negotiation:** Pre-MBA salaries anchor post-MBA offers despite marginal relevance; women are less inclined to negotiate aggressively (Bowles, Babcock, & McGinn, 2005), resulting in lower salary anchors
- **Nisbett and Ross (1980):** The anchoring bias itself makes it difficult to convince people to change their decision-making strategies -- existing heuristics are cognitive anchors

## Ariely Extensions (Predictably Irrational)

Ariely's experiments extend anchoring into the concept of arbitrary-coherence -- the idea that initial prices are arbitrary but become coherent reference points for all future valuations (summary-2-S1-pi-ch2-supply-demand):

- **SSN anchoring experiment (Ariely, Prelec, & Loewenstein):** N=55 MIT MBA students. Last two digits of social security number served as price anchors for 6 products. Students with SSN 80-99 bid **216-346% higher** than those with SSN 00-19. Correlations: 0.32-0.52. Yet relative pricing within categories was coherent (everyone bid more for better wine) -- the anchor was arbitrary but created a coherent price structure.
- **Annoying sounds experiment:** First anchor (10 cents vs. 90 cents) persisted across three subsequent sounds and **resisted replacement by new anchors** -- demonstrating that initial anchors have durable, cross-decision effects.
- **Poetry reading experiment:** Whether an ambiguous experience was anchored as "worth paying for" or "requiring compensation" completely determined subsequent valuation patterns.
- **Housing market anchoring (Simonsohn & Loewenstein):** People who move cities remain anchored to their previous city's housing prices -- spending similar amounts regardless of the new market.
- These findings extend anchoring from a one-shot estimation error to a **persistent force shaping long-term consumption patterns** through self-herding.

## Open Questions
- How strong is anchoring when the anchor is obviously absurd? (Bazerman confirms: still remarkably strong -- even subliminal anchors work per Mussweiler & Englich, 2005)
- Is anchoring primarily a failure of adjustment or a priming/accessibility effect? (Epley, 2004 clarifies: both mechanisms operate, depending on whether the anchor is externally imposed or self-generated)
- Can training or debiasing techniques reduce anchoring? (Evidence is mixed -- awareness helps somewhat but doesn't eliminate the effect)
- How can organizations design systems that minimize the influence of irrelevant anchors on important decisions?

relatedSummaries.title: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases — Summary
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman
**Type:** Seminal research paper
**Published:** *Science*, Vol. 185, No. 4157, September 27, 1974, pp. 1124–1131
**Phase:** 1 — Cognitive Foundations
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-13

## Key Takeaways

1. People rely on a small number of **heuristic principles** to reduce complex probability judgments to simpler operations. These are generally useful but lead to **systematic and predictable errors**.
2. Three heuristics are identified: **representativeness**, **availability**, and **anchoring-and-adjustment**.
3. These biases are not attributable to motivational factors (wishful thinking, payoffs/penalties) — they are **cognitive**, found even in experienced researchers and statisticians.
4. Subjective probabilities systematically deviate from normative probability theory, and this has implications for any domain relying on human judgment under uncertainty.

## Detailed Notes

### The Central Thesis

Many decisions depend on beliefs about the likelihood of uncertain events. People assess these probabilities not through formal calculation but through heuristics — mental shortcuts. These heuristics are "quite useful, but sometimes they lead to severe and systematic errors." The biases are not random noise; they are predictable and directional.

### Heuristic 1: Representativeness

People assess the probability that object A belongs to class B (or that event A originates from process B) by evaluating **how much A resembles B** — how "representative" it is.

**Biases produced by representativeness:**

- **Insensitivity to prior probabilities (base rates).** When given a personality description of "Steve" (shy, helpful, meek, tidy, need for order), subjects judged the probability he was a librarian vs. farmer vs. pilot etc. based entirely on how much he resembled the stereotype — ignoring that there are far more farmers than librarians. Prior probabilities should matter enormously but were effectively discarded. Even when base rates were explicitly provided, subjects largely ignored them unless no other information was available.

- **Insensitivity to sample size.** Subjects failed to appreciate that small samples are more variable than large ones. When told a hospital has ~45 births/day vs. ~15 births/day and asked which would more often record >60% boys, most said "about the same." The correct answer is the smaller hospital, because small samples deviate more from the population mean. The "law of large numbers" was not intuitively applied.

- **Misconceptions of chance.** People expect random sequences to "look random" even in short runs. The sequence H-T-H-T-T-H is judged more likely than H-H-H-T-T-T (which looks too ordered) or H-H-H-H-T-H (which doesn't look fair). This is the **gamblers-fallacy** — expecting short sequences to be self-correcting. Tversky and Kahneman call this the "law of small numbers": the belief that small samples should mirror the population.

- **Insensitivity to predictability.** When given a favorable description of a company, subjects predicted high profits regardless of whether the description was known to be reliable. The favorableness of the input dominates the prediction; its reliability is neglected. Predictions should regress toward the mean when predictability is low, but people make extreme predictions even from weak evidence.

- **The illusion of validity.** People express high confidence in predictions based on input that is "representative" even when they know the input has low validity. Redundancy among inputs *increases* subjective confidence (the pattern seems more consistent) while actually *decreasing* accuracy (correlated inputs provide less independent information). Experienced clinicians, interviewers, and judges all show this pattern — confident predictions from weak data.

- **Misconceptions of regression.** People fail to recognize regression to the mean. When extreme performance is followed by average performance, people invent causal explanations (the instructor who praised good landings and then saw worse ones concluded praise was harmful; the one who criticized bad landings and saw improvement concluded criticism was effective). The phenomenon of regression remains "elusive" because it is incompatible with the belief that the predicted outcome should be maximally representative of the input.

### Heuristic 2: Availability

People assess the frequency or probability of an event by **how easily instances come to mind** — how "available" they are in memory.

**Biases produced by availability:**

- **Biases due to retrievability of instances.** If instances of a class are easily retrieved, that class is judged as more frequent. Familiarity, salience, and recency all affect retrieval. Example: subjects judged whether a list had more men or women — the list with famous names (of one gender) was judged to have more of that gender, regardless of actual count. The fame made those names more retrievable.

- **Biases due to effectiveness of a search set.** The cognitive structure of the search matters. Example: people judge words beginning with "r" as more common than words with "r" in the third position — because it's easier to search memory by first letter. In reality, "r" in third position is more common. The search strategy creates the bias.

- **Biases of imaginability.** When people must assess likelihood by mentally constructing scenarios, the ease of construction dominates. Example: how many committees of 2 can be formed from 10 people vs. committees of 8? People estimate far more committees of 2, because small groups are easier to imagine — but the correct answers are identical (both = 45).

- **Illusory correlation.** When two events are "associatively connected" (e.g., suspiciousness and peculiar eye drawings in diagnostic projective tests), people overestimate how often they co-occur. Chapman and Chapman showed that both naive subjects and experienced clinicians "rediscovered" correlations that had no basis in data, purely because the pairing seemed natural. Even when shown data where the correlation was actually *negative*, the illusory correlation persisted.

### Heuristic 3: Adjustment and Anchoring

People make estimates by **starting from an initial value and adjusting** — but adjustments are typically **insufficient**, so the final answer is biased toward the anchor.

**Biases produced by anchoring:**

- **Insufficient adjustment.** Subjects who watched a random wheel of fortune spin to 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the UN, gave median estimates of 25 and 45 respectively — massively different answers anchored by an obviously random number. Even with incentives for accuracy, anchoring persisted.

- **Biases in evaluation of conjunctive and disjunctive events.** People overestimate conjunctive probabilities (the probability that ALL of a series of likely events occur) and underestimate disjunctive probabilities (the probability that AT LEAST ONE of a series of unlikely events occurs). Example: subjects preferred betting on 7 successive successes at 90% each (conjunctive — actual probability 48%) over a single event at 50%, and preferred a single event at 50% over at least one success in 7 tries at 10% each (disjunctive — actual probability 52%). This has practical consequences: project planning is conjunctive (everything must go right), leading to overoptimism; risk assessment is disjunctive (any component can fail), leading to underestimation of risk.

- **Anchoring in assessment of subjective probability distributions.** When asked to set confidence intervals (e.g., the 1st and 99th percentile for the Dow-Jones average), people set ranges far too narrow. The true values fell outside stated 98% confidence intervals roughly 30% of the time, not 2%. Two procedures were tested — setting extremes first vs. setting a best estimate first — and both showed severe overconfidence, though the latter was somewhat worse.

### The Nature of These Biases

The paper emphasizes several critical points about the biases:

1. **Not motivational.** These are cognitive errors, not wishful thinking. They appear in problems with no stakes and no emotional content.
2. **Resistant to expertise.** Experienced researchers, statisticians, and trained professionals show the same biases. Even people with "extensive training in statistics" have intuitive judgments "liable to similar fallacies in more intricate and less transparent problems."
3. **Systematic, not random.** The errors are predictable in direction and magnitude, which means they can be studied, anticipated, and potentially corrected.
4. **Practically consequential.** The paper's closing argues that understanding these heuristics "could improve judgments and decisions in situations of uncertainty."

## New Entities Introduced
- tversky — Amos Tversky, cognitive psychologist, Hebrew University / Stanford
- kahneman — Daniel Kahneman, cognitive psychologist, Hebrew University / Princeton

## New Concepts Introduced
- representativeness — Heuristic: judging probability by similarity/resemblance
- availability — Heuristic: judging frequency/probability by ease of recall
- anchoring-and-adjustment — Heuristic: estimating by adjusting from an initial value
- base-rate-neglect — Ignoring prior probabilities when representativeness information is present
- law-of-small-numbers — Expecting small samples to mirror population properties
- gamblers-fallacy — Expecting random sequences to be self-correcting
- illusion-of-validity — Unwarranted confidence in predictions from representative but low-validity inputs
- regression-to-the-mean — Extreme values tend to be followed by less extreme ones; people fail to recognize this
- illusory-correlation — Overestimating co-occurrence of associatively linked events
- overconfidence-in-calibration — Setting confidence intervals far too narrow

## Contradictions or Tensions
- None with existing wiki content (this is the first source ingested).
- Internal tension worth noting: the paper claims these biases are "not attributable to motivational effects" but later research (including by Kahneman himself) explores how motivation and emotion *do* interact with heuristic processing. This will likely be revisited in later Phase 1 and Phase 2 sources.

## Quotes Worth Keeping

> "People rely on a limited number of heuristic principles which reduce the complex tasks of assessing probabilities and predicting values to simpler judgmental operations. In general, these heuristics are quite useful, but sometimes they lead to severe and systematic errors." — Tversky & Kahneman, p. 1124

> "The subjects' willingness to deduce the likelihood of a particular event from prior events was unrelated to their willingness to use the same prior events to generate probabilistic estimates." — paraphrased from base-rate neglect section

> "The notion that sampling variance decreases in proportion to sample size is apparently not part of people's repertoire of intuitions." — p. 1125

> "The production of a compelling scenario is likely to constrain future thinking. There is much evidence showing that, once an uncertain situation has been perceived or interpreted in a particular fashion, it is quite difficult to view it in any other way." — p. 1127 (on availability and imaginability)

> "In his evaluation of evidence, man is apparently not a conservative Bayesian: he is not Bayesian at all." — p. 1124 (on representativeness and base-rate neglect)

> "Subjective probabilities... are not 'conservative' as a chance process model would predict; they are nearly always more extreme." — p. 1129 (on anchoring and overconfidence)

relatedSummaries.title: Social Psychology Ch.4: Social Perception — Summary
relatedSummaries.authors: Elliot Aronson, Timothy Wilson, Robin Akert
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Elliot Aronson, Timothy Wilson, Robin Akert
**Type:** Textbook chapter (Chapter 4: Social Perception)
**Published:** *Social Psychology*, Pearson (10th edition)
**Phase:** 1 — Cognitive Foundations
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-13

## Key Takeaways

1. **Social perception is how we form impressions of and make inferences about other people** — relying on nonverbal communication, first impressions, and causal attribution.
2. **The fundamental attribution error (FAE)** is the central bias in social perception: we overestimate dispositional causes and underestimate situational causes of others' behavior. This is arguably the most important single concept in social psychology.
3. **First impressions form in under 100 milliseconds** and persist through primacy effects and belief perseverance — making the opening moments of any interaction disproportionately powerful.
4. **Culture profoundly shapes social perception** — Western individualistic cultures favor dispositional attributions (analytic thinking), while East Asian collectivistic cultures favor situational attributions (holistic thinking). This is not inborn but learned.
5. **People are systematically bad at recognizing their own biases** — the bias blind spot means we see others as biased but ourselves as rational.

## Detailed Notes

### Section 1: Nonverbal Communication (LO 4.1)

**nonverbal-communication** — how people communicate intentionally or unintentionally without words. Channels include facial expressions, tone of voice, gestures, body position, eye gaze, touch, and personal space.

**Facial Expressions of Emotion:**
- Darwin (1872) proposed facial expressions are universal, evolutionary vestiges of once-useful physiological reactions
- Paul Ekman and Walter Friesen (1971) confirmed this with the South Fore tribe in New Guinea — a preliterate people with no Western contact could match facial expressions to emotional stories with the same accuracy as Western subjects
- **Six universal emotions:** anger, happiness, surprise, fear, disgust, sadness (possibly also pride, contempt, anxiety, shame, embarrassment)
- **Affect blends:** one part of the face registers one emotion, another part registers a different emotion — making decoding harder
- Susskind et al. (2008): fear face *enhances* sensory input (wider eyes, more air intake); disgust face *reduces* it — functional evolutionary design

**Complications in decoding:**
- Context matters: the same facial expression has different implications depending on eye gaze direction (Adams & Kleck, 2003) and surrounding people's expressions (Masuda et al., 2008)
- Culture matters: Japanese participants interpreted emotion in context (holistic); Americans focused on the individual face alone (analytic)

**Culture and Nonverbal Channels:**
- **Display rules** (Ekman): culturally determined norms about which emotional expressions are appropriate. Japanese norms suppress negative expressions; American norms suppress male grief/crying.
- **Emblems:** gestures with well-defined meanings within a culture (OK sign, thumbs up) — but these are NOT universal and can cause cross-cultural miscommunication
- Personal space norms vary dramatically across cultures (Hall, 1969)

### Section 2: First Impressions — Quick But Long-Lasting (LO 4.2)

**thin-slicing** (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992, 1993):
- People form impressions from extremely brief behavioral samples
- Impressions form in **under 100 milliseconds** based on facial appearance alone (Bar, Neta, & Linz, 2006; Willis & Todorov, 2006)
- Children as young as 3 show this tendency (Cogsdill et al., 2014)
- Thin-sliced impressions of teachers from 10-second silent video clips **correlated significantly** with end-of-semester evaluations from students who spent months with those teachers
- Baby-face effect: people with childlike features (big eyes, small chin) are perceived as naive, warm, submissive
- Political candidates who *look* more powerful are more likely to win elections (Rule & Ambady, 2010; Todorov et al., 2008)

**primacy-effect** (Asch, 1946):
- The classic demonstration: "intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious" produces a more positive impression than the same traits in reverse order
- First information creates a **schema** through which all subsequent information is filtered
- "What is beautiful is good" — physical attractiveness creates a halo effect (Dion, Berscheid, & Walster, 1972)

**belief-perseverance:**
- People stick with initial judgments even when the evidence is contradicted or retracted (Anderson, 1995; Ross, Lepper, & Hubbard, 1975)
- Explains why jurors can't disregard ruled-inadmissible evidence, why discredited research persists, why debunked political misinformation keeps working
- Connection to cognitive dissonance: "we find inconsistent thoughts unpleasant and uncomfortable"

**Practical implications:** First impressions in presentations, job interviews, and meetings are disproportionately important. The opening moments set a frame that is extremely hard to overcome.

### Section 3: Causal Attribution — Answering the "Why" Question (LO 4.3)

**attribution-theory** (Heider, 1958):
- Fritz Heider: people are "naive scientists" who try to understand behavior by inferring causes
- The fundamental dichotomy: **internal attribution** (disposition, personality, character) vs. **external attribution** (situation, context, circumstance)
- Which attribution we make profoundly shapes our impression of the person
- In relationships: happy spouses make internal attributions for partner's positive behavior and external attributions for negative behavior; distressed spouses do the opposite

**covariation-model** (Kelley, 1967):
- To determine internal vs. external attribution, we assess three dimensions:
  - **Consensus:** Do other people behave the same way toward this stimulus?
  - **Distinctiveness:** Does this person behave this way toward other stimuli?
  - **Consistency:** Does this person behave this way toward this stimulus across time?
- **Internal attribution** when: low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency (only this person, acts this way with everyone, does it every time)
- **External attribution** when: high consensus + high distinctiveness + high consistency (everyone reacts this way, only to this stimulus, every time)
- Limitation: people underuse consensus information and don't always have all three dimensions available

**fundamental-attribution-error** (Ross, 1977) / Correspondence Bias:
- The tendency to **overestimate internal, dispositional factors and underestimate situational factors** when explaining others' behavior
- **Jones & Harris (1967) Castro essay study:** Even when told the essay writer was *assigned* a position (pro- or anti-Castro), participants still believed the essay reflected the writer's true beliefs. Knowing the situation didn't eliminate the dispositional inference.
- **Why it happens — perceptual-salience:** People are perceptually prominent; situations are invisible. We see the person, not the context. Taylor & Fiske (1975) showed that whichever actor observers could see better was judged as more influential — same conversation, different attributions based on viewing angle.
- **Lassiter et al. (2007):** Camera angle on videotaped confessions affects perceived voluntariness — even judges and police officers rated confessions as more voluntary when the camera focused only on the suspect. New Zealand adopted equal-focus camera rules in direct response.
- **Two-step attribution process (Gilbert, 1989):** Step 1 is automatic — make an internal attribution. Step 2 is effortful — adjust for the situation. We often don't complete Step 2, especially when distracted, busy, or cognitively loaded. This connects directly to anchoring-and-adjustment from 1-01.

**self-serving-attribution:**
- Take credit for successes (internal attribution); blame failures on external factors
- Athletes: 80% of attributions for wins were internal; losses were attributed to external causes (Lau & Russell, 1980)
- Less experienced athletes make stronger self-serving attributions; experienced athletes are more balanced
- Motivated by: self-esteem maintenance, impression management, and differential information access (you know your own effort and ability better than an observer does)

**just-world-belief** (Lerner, 1980):
- The assumption that people get what they deserve and deserve what they get
- A **defensive attribution** — believing the world is just protects the belief that bad things won't happen to us
- Leads to **victim blaming** — victims of crimes and accidents are seen as somehow responsible for their fate
- More common in cultures with extreme wealth inequality; connected to karma in Hindu/Buddhist traditions

**bias-blind-spot** (Pronin et al., 2002):
- People rate themselves as "somewhat" susceptible to biases but rate the "average American" as much more susceptible
- An ironic self-serving belief: "I'm rational, but other people are biased"
- Implications: awareness of biases doesn't automatically protect against them

### Section 4: Culture and Social Perception (LO 4.4)

**Individualistic vs. Collectivistic Cultures:**
- Western cultures stress individual autonomy → **analytic thinking style** (focus on the object/person, ignore context)
- East Asian cultures stress group harmony → **holistic thinking style** (focus on the whole picture, object + context + relationships)
- Masuda et al. (2008): Americans judged a cartoon character's emotion from the character alone; Japanese were significantly influenced by surrounding characters' expressions. Eye-tracking confirmed Japanese scanned the background more.
- Neuroscience (Hedden et al., 2008): fMRI showed Americans needed more brain activation to attend to context; East Asians needed more to ignore context — the default mode differs by culture.

**Cultural differences in FAE:**
- Miller (1984): Americans made dispositional attributions for Indian-generated behavior examples; Indians made situational attributions for the same behaviors. Children from both cultures were indistinguishable — the difference is learned, not inborn.
- Hong et al. (2003): Bicultural Hong Kong students primed with American images made more dispositional attributions; primed with Chinese images, more situational. Cultural thinking styles can be activated by priming.

**Cultural differences in self-serving bias:**
- Meta-analysis of 266 studies (Mezulis et al., 2004): Self-serving bias strongest in US, Canada, Australia, NZ. Weaker in Japan, Pacific Islands, India.
- In collectivistic cultures: success is attributed to others (teachers, parents, situation); failure is attributed to self (self-criticism as social glue)
- Media coverage reflects this: American Olympic coverage focused on individual talent; Japanese coverage included coaches, family, and circumstances

## New Entities Introduced
- aronson — Elliot Aronson, social psychologist, textbook author
- heider — Fritz Heider, father of attribution theory
- asch — Solomon Asch, pioneered impression formation research

## New Concepts Introduced
- nonverbal-communication — Communication without words: facial expressions, gestures, gaze, touch, space
- thin-slicing — Forming meaningful impressions from extremely brief behavioral samples
- primacy-effect — First information disproportionately shapes subsequent interpretation
- belief-perseverance — Sticking with initial judgments despite contradicting evidence
- attribution-theory — How people explain the causes of behavior (internal vs. external)
- covariation-model — Kelley's framework: consensus, distinctiveness, consistency → attribution
- fundamental-attribution-error — Overestimating dispositional causes, underestimating situational causes
- perceptual-salience — What we attend to seems more causally important
- self-serving-attribution — Credit for success (internal), blame for failure (external)
- just-world-belief — Assumption that people get what they deserve
- bias-blind-spot — Believing others are more biased than we are

## Contradictions or Tensions
- **With 1-01 (Heuristics paper):** The FAE can be understood as a specific instance of anchoring-and-adjustment — the initial dispositional attribution is the anchor, and situational adjustment is insufficient (Gilbert's two-step model explicitly makes this connection).
- **Cultural moderation of biases:** 1-01 and 1-02 present biases as universal cognitive features. This chapter shows that the FAE and self-serving bias vary significantly by culture — the biases are not equally strong everywhere. This doesn't invalidate them but adds an important moderator.
- **Thin-slicing accuracy vs. biases:** There's a tension between the finding that thin-sliced impressions can be remarkably accurate (Ambady) and the finding that first impressions are biased by irrelevant features (baby-face, attractiveness halo). Thin-slicing works when the cues are genuinely informative but misleads when they trigger stereotypes.

## Quotes Worth Keeping

> "The fundamental theory or schema most of us have about human behavior is that people do what they do because of the kind of people they are, not because of the situation they are in." — Aronson, Wilson, Akert

> "We focus our attention more on the person than on the surrounding situation because the situation is so hard to see or know." — on perceptual salience and the FAE

> "Cross-cultural differences in social perception do not appear to be inborn; rather, we arrive in this world with a flexibility of thinking style that is molded over time by cultural (and other) influences." — on Miller's (1984) finding that children from US and India were indistinguishable

> "I think I just stayed focused. It was time to show the world what I could do." — Misty Hyman, American gold medalist (dispositional attribution)
> "Here is the best coach in the world, the best manager in the world, and all of the people who support me — all these things were getting together and became a gold medal." — Naoko Takahashi, Japanese gold medalist (situational attribution)

relatedSummaries.title: For Those Condemned to Study the Past: Heuristics and Biases in Hindsight — Summary
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Baruch Fischhoff
**Type:** Research paper (Chapter 23 in *Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases*)
**Published:** 1982, in Kahneman, Slovic, & Tversky (Eds.), Cambridge University Press
**Phase:** 2 — Decision Science
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. **Hindsight bias** ("I knew it all along"): People consistently exaggerate what could have been anticipated in foresight once they know the outcome. They view what happened as having been inevitable and misremember their own prior predictions to align with known outcomes.
2. Fischhoff introduces the term **creeping determinism** -- the unconscious tendency to view reported outcomes as having been relatively inevitable, distinct from philosophical determinism (the conscious belief that everything is predetermined).
3. The paper goes far beyond demonstrating a single bias. It provides a sweeping analysis of how retrospection systematically misleads: we find spurious patterns in randomness, overfit explanations to data, confuse tactical with strategic wisdom, and fail to learn from the past precisely because hindsight makes the past seem transparent.
4. **Warning people about hindsight bias has little effect.** The more effective remedy is forcing oneself to argue against the inevitability of the known outcome -- and even this is only partially successful.

## Detailed Notes

### Looking for Wisdom: The Pitfalls of Regression Modeling

Fischhoff begins by examining formal attempts to extract wisdom from the past (regression modeling, policy-capturing studies). Key problems:

- **Multicollinearity** makes regression weights uninterpretable -- the shared explanatory capacity between correlated predictors is divided arbitrarily.
- Two decades of clinical judgment research reveal a "disturbing pair of conclusions": (a) simple linear models excellently predict judges' decisions, but (b) judges claim they use much more complex strategies (configural judgment). The judges are wrong about their own processes.
- Simple linear models are "extraordinarily powerful predictors" -- a theme Fischhoff attributes to and cross-references with Dawes (Chapter 28). Even a simple count of encouraging vs. discouraging signs provides a good prediction.
- The power of regression modeling tempts us to embrace complicated theories whose real explanatory power comes from very simple underlying notions.

### Looking for Folly: The Asymmetry of Error Analysis

Studying failures systematically misleads because:

- **Focus on failure** inflates the perceived frequency of misfortune via availability. Dramatic failures are memorable; unremarkable successes are "uneventful."
- **Error asymmetry is unintuitive.** Any imperfect decision system produces both false positives and false negatives. Before condemning a system for allowing some cheaters, one should ask whether the ratio of commission to omission errors is actually too high.
- **Tactical vs. strategic distinction.** Many apparent errors are actually "deft resolution of the wrong problem." Ford's Pinto fuel tank decision was tactically rational (saving $15 per car across 10 million cars) but strategically foolish (ignoring non-economic reputational consequences). Banks appear wise at repetitive tactical decisions (mortgages, insurance) where they virtually cannot lose, but are "no smarter than the rest of us" at strategic decisions requiring analytical judgment.

### Hindsight: Thinking Backward

The paper's core contribution. Key findings from Fischhoff's prior experimental work:

- **People exaggerate foresight.** After learning an outcome, people believe they would have predicted it. They view outcomes as having appeared "relatively inevitable" even before they happened.
- **Misremembering predictions.** People misremember their own prior predictions so as to align with the known outcome (Fischhoff & Beyth, 1975).
- **Telescoping.** People exaggerate the speed of "inevitable" historical changes. Example: people can point to the moment the latifundia were doomed, without realizing they took two and a half centuries to disappear.
- **Remembering people wrong.** People remember others as having been more like their current selves than was actually the case (Yarrow, Campbell, & Burton, 1970).
- **Myth of the critical experiment.** Critical experiments are recognized as critical only decades later -- in real time, theories resist falsification and accommodate anomalies.

### Consequences for Learning

Hindsight bias is not merely a curiosity; it has devastating consequences for learning from experience:

1. **Self-blame without improvement.** Decision makers who re-create their pre-outcome state of mind find the outcome "should have been obvious" -- they berate themselves without understanding what actually went wrong. "They add the insult of regret to the injury inflicted by the event itself."
2. **Unfair second-guessing.** Hindsightful observers see incompetence where there was merely the inevitable uncertainty of a fallible system.
3. **Weak hypothesis testing.** If past events seem to have been predictable, our explanatory hypotheses face inordinately weak tests. We find little reason to update our theories.
4. **The paradox:** "The very outcome knowledge which gives us the feeling that we understand what the past was all about may prevent us from learning anything from it."

### The Mechanism

Fischhoff explains the psychological process: upon receiving outcome knowledge, we immediately integrate it into our existing understanding, reinterpreting the situation so the outcome seems like a natural outgrowth. This reinterpretation happens automatically and we are often unaware of it. When trying to reconstruct our pre-outcome mental state, we remain "anchored in our hindsightful perspective" -- the outcome remains "too likely looking."

This connects directly to anchoring-and-adjustment: even deliberate attempts to undo the effect of outcome knowledge leave a residual anchor.

### Looking at All: Finding Patterns in Noise

The paper's broadest section examines our tendency to find order in randomness:

- **gamblers-fallacy extended.** Random processes are interpreted as purposeful. Morrison (1977) claimed Roosevelt's court-packing effort was unnecessary because "the odds were eleven to one" he would get a vacancy that year -- but this reasoning incorrectly assumes a random process "remembers" previous outcomes.
- **London Blitz.** Londoners developed elaborate theories about German bombing patterns; the actual distribution of bomb-hits was almost perfectly Poisson (random).
- **regression-to-the-mean ignored.** Athletes criticized for poor performance tend to improve next time -- confirming our theory that punishment works, when it is merely regression. Stock analysts explain every price movement, including those from a random walk process.

### Overfitting

Fischhoff articulates a powerful analogy between statistical overfitting and narrative explanation:

- Given enough possible explanatory factors, any event can be "explained" to any desired degree of tightness.
- "An overfitted theory is like a suit tailored so precisely to one individual in one particular pose that it will not fit anyone else."
- Historians build "airtight" cases using available evidence; the release of suppressed documents would collapse the theory.
- Investment analysts overfit and pay the price with long-run failure to outperform market averages.

### Remedies

- **Warning alone does not work** (Fischhoff, 1977b).
- **Arguing against inevitability** -- forcing oneself to explain how it might have turned out otherwise -- is somewhat effective (Koriat, Lichtenstein, & Fischhoff, 1980).
- **Tracking down original uncertainty** -- finding contemporaneous records (transcripts, notebooks, diaries) that capture the confusion that existed before the outcome.
- **Making predictions** that can be evaluated, and keeping records of deliberations before decisions.
- **Using multiple perspectives** -- no single method is adequate; use as broad a range of techniques as possible.

## New Entities Introduced

- fischhoff -- Baruch Fischhoff, decision researcher, Carnegie Mellon University

## New Concepts Introduced

- hindsight-bias -- Exaggerating in retrospect what could have been anticipated in foresight; believing outcomes were inevitable
- creeping-determinism -- The unconscious tendency to view reported outcomes as having been relatively inevitable, distinct from philosophical determinism

## Contradictions or Tensions

- Fischhoff's analysis of overfitting and narrative coherence anticipates what Nassim Taleb later calls the "narrative fallacy." The wiki does not yet have a page for this concept.
- The connection between hindsight bias and anchoring-and-adjustment is explicit: our hindsightful perspective serves as an anchor from which we insufficiently adjust when trying to reconstruct foresight.
- Fischhoff references Dawes (Ch. 28) approvingly regarding the power of simple linear models vs. clinical judgment, establishing a direct intellectual link between these two papers.

## Quotes Worth Keeping

> "In hindsight, people consistently exaggerate what could have been anticipated in foresight. They not only tend to view what has happened as having been inevitable but also to view it as having appeared 'relatively inevitable' before it happened." — Fischhoff, p. 341

> "The very outcome knowledge which gives us the feeling that we understand what the past was all about may prevent us from learning anything from it." — Fischhoff, p. 343

> "An overfitted theory is like a suit tailored so precisely to one individual in one particular pose that it will not fit anyone else or even that same individual in the future or even in the present if new evidence about him comes to light." — Fischhoff, p. 349

> "Merely warning people about the dangers of hindsight bias has little effect." — Fischhoff, p. 343

> "The historian who is most conscious of his own situation is also most capable of transcending it." — Benedetto Croce, quoted by Fischhoff, p. 355

relatedSummaries.title: Intuitive Prediction: Biases and Corrective Procedures — Summary
relatedSummaries.source: 2-06 - Judgment Under Uncertainty - Heuristics and Biases (Collection) - Kahneman, Slovic, Tversky
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky
**Type:** Research chapter (Chapter 30 in *Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases*)
**Published:** 1982, in Kahneman, Slovic, & Tversky (Eds.), Cambridge University Press
**Phase:** 2 -- Decision Science
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. **Intuitive predictions are typically nonregressive** -- people match their prediction to their impression of the case rather than adjusting toward the base rate, producing predictions that are systematically too extreme.
2. **Singular vs. distributional information**: Forecasters rely excessively on singular (case-specific) information and underweight distributional (base-rate) data, even when distributional data are available and more reliable.
3. **The planning fallacy** is a direct consequence of neglecting distributional information: people underestimate completion times because they focus on the internal features of the specific project rather than the distribution of outcomes in similar past projects.
4. **A five-step corrective procedure** can guide experts toward properly regressive predictions: (1) select a reference class, (2) assess its distribution, (3) make an intuitive estimate, (4) assess predictability, and (5) correct the intuitive estimate toward the mean.
5. **The key insight**: Intuitive predictions contain useful information but are biased in predictable ways; the solution is not to reject them but to debias them by integrating distributional data.

## Detailed Notes

### Singular and Distributional Data

Experts making predictions have access to two types of information:
- **Singular information** (case data): evidence about the particular case -- the author's style, the student's GPA, the patient's symptoms
- **Distributional information** (base-rate data): knowledge about the distribution of outcomes in similar cases -- how books of this type typically sell, how students with these credentials typically perform

The concept of distributional data does not coincide with the Bayesian concept of a prior probability distribution. Distributional data is defined by the nature of the data; prior probabilities are defined by the sequence of information acquisition.

Many prediction problems are essentially unique (e.g., forecasting nuclear energy demand in 2000, when a cure for leukemia will be found), making distributional data unavailable. In such cases, experts must rely on singular information. However, the evidence suggests that people are **insufficiently sensitive to distributional data even when such data are available** -- they rely primarily on singular information even when it is scanty and unreliable (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973; Tversky & Kahneman, Ch. 10).

### The Planning Fallacy

The context of planning provides many examples of distributional neglect:
- Scientists and writers are notoriously prone to underestimate completion time despite considerable experience of past failures
- Engineers underestimate repair times for power stations (Kidd, 1970)
- The planning fallacy is sometimes attributable to motivational factors (wishful thinking) but frequently occurs even when underestimation is penalized

The planning fallacy arises from an **internal approach** to prediction -- focusing on the specific problem's constituents rather than the distribution of outcomes in similar cases. The internal approach produces underestimation because a building can only be completed on time if there are no delays, no strikes, no unusual weather, etc. Each disruption is individually unlikely, but the combinatorial probability that at least one will occur is substantial (Bar-Hillel, 1973). Adjusting by a "slippage factor" fails because the adjusted value remains anchored too close to the initial estimate (anchoring-and-adjustment).

The **external approach** treats the specific problem as one of many: "How long do such projects usually last?" rather than "What are the specific factors in this project?" More reasonable estimates are likely from the external question.

The tendency to neglect distributional information is enhanced by:
- Perceived uniqueness of the problem
- Detailed acquaintance with the specific case
- Intense involvement
- The formulation of the question (asking about total cost induces internal thinking; asking about percentage of cost overruns invokes distributional thinking)

### Regression and Intuitive Prediction

In most prediction problems, the expert has both singular and distributional information. Psychological research (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973; Ross, 1977) suggests intuitive predictions follow a **simple matching rule**: the predicted value is selected so that the standing of the case in the distribution of outcomes matches its standing in the distribution of impressions.

**Example:** An editor reviews a novel manuscript and says: "This book reads like a best-seller. Among books of this type published in recent years, only one in twenty impressed me more." If asked to predict sales, the editor would likely predict top 5% of the distribution.

This matching rule is unsound because it **fails to take uncertainty into account.** When predictability is low (as in book sales), the best prediction should fall between the impression-matched value and the class average. The lower the predictability, the closer the prediction should be to the class average. Intuitive predictions are typically nonregressive: people make extreme predictions on the basis of information whose reliability and predictive validity are known to be low.

### A Corrective Procedure for Prediction

Kahneman and Tversky propose a **five-step corrective procedure**:

**Step 1: Selection of a reference class.** Identify a class to which the case can be meaningfully referred and for which the distribution of outcomes is known. The choice involves trade-offs: the most inclusive class allows the best estimate of the distribution, but may be too heterogeneous for meaningful comparison. The class of books by the same author provides the most natural comparison, but the book in question may fall outside previously observed ranges.

**Step 2: Assessment of the distribution for the reference class.** The expert should provide an estimate of the class average and the range of variability. For long-term forecasting where direct distributional data are unavailable, the distribution can sometimes be estimated indirectly (e.g., England's share of world market in various technologies as a proxy for a specific technology).

**Step 3: Intuitive estimation.** The expert makes an intuitive estimate based on singular information about the particular case. This estimate is likely to be nonregressive -- the next two steps correct for this.

**Step 4: Assessment of predictability.** The expert assesses the degree to which the available information permits accurate prediction. In linear prediction, the appropriate measure is the product-moment correlation between predictions and outcomes. Methods for assessing predictability:
- Direct subjective estimate of the correlation coefficient (for statistically sophisticated experts)
- Ordinal comparison: "If you were to consider two novels you are about to publish, how often would you be right in predicting which will sell more copies?" If the estimated proportion correct is q, then tau = 2q - 1 provides a crude approximation for the correlation.
- Comparing predictability to other domains (e.g., sales of books vs. point spreads in football vs. weather forecasting)

**Caution:** Estimates of predictability should be examined carefully. The expert may be subject to the hindsight-bias (Fischhoff, 1975), overestimating predictability of outcomes, or to availability bias, recalling primarily memorable cases where strong impressions were confirmed.

**Step 5: Correction of the intuitive estimate.** To correct for nonregressiveness, adjust the intuitive estimate toward the reference class average. If the estimate was nonregressive, the distance between the intuitive estimate and the class average should be reduced by a factor of the correlation coefficient (rho).

**Example:** Expert's intuitive prediction of book sales = 12,000 copies. Class average = 4,000 copies. Expert believes he would correctly rank pairs 80% of the time, so tau = 1.6 - 1 = 0.6. Regressed estimate = 4,000 + 0.6(12,000 - 4,000) = **8,800 copies**.

The effect of this correction is substantial when the intuitive estimate is relatively extreme or predictability is moderate to low.

### Objections and Responses

**Objection 1:** The expert may question the assumption that his initial estimate was nonregressive. This can be verified by asking the expert to estimate (a) the proportion of cases that would have made a stronger impression and (b) the proportion for which the outcome exceeds the prediction. If these proportions are approximately equal, the prediction is surely nonregressive.

**Objection 2:** Predictions should not be regressive because they yield conservative predictions near the class average and cannot predict exceptional outcomes. Response: A fallible predictor can retain a chance to correctly predict exceptional outcomes only at the cost of erroneously identifying many other cases as exceptional. Nonregressive predictions over-predict: any high prediction is associated with a substantial probability of being an overestimate, and any low prediction is an underestimate. In most situations, this bias is costly and should be eliminated.

### Concluding Remarks

The approach is based on three notions about forecasting: (1) most predictions and forecasts contain an irreducible intuitive component, (2) intuitive predictions of knowledgeable individuals contain much useful information, (3) these intuitive judgments are often biased in a predictable manner. The problem is not whether to accept or reject intuitive predictions, but how to debias and improve them.

The strategy of debiasing elicits from the expert relevant information that he would normally neglect and helps him integrate this information with his intuitive impressions in a manner that respects basic principles of statistical prediction.

## New Concepts Introduced

- regression-prediction -- The principle that optimal predictions should be regressive (pulled toward the base rate), with the degree of regression determined by the predictability of the criterion

## Cross-References

- base-rate-neglect -- The core bias underlying nonregressive prediction
- representativeness -- The heuristic that drives the matching rule (prediction matches impression)
- anchoring-and-adjustment -- Planning fallacy arises from insufficient adjustment from internal estimates
- regression-to-the-mean -- The statistical principle that predictions should respect
- hindsight-bias -- Can distort experts' assessments of their own predictive accuracy
- availability -- Can bias experts' recall of prediction successes and failures
- debiasing-strategies -- The five-step procedure is a structured debiasing technique
- clinical-vs-statistical-prediction -- The corrective procedure bridges clinical (intuitive) and statistical approaches
- summary-2-06-hb-ch18-clinical-reasoning -- Eddy demonstrates the same base-rate neglect in medical prediction
- summary-2-06-hb-ch28-improper-linear-models -- Dawes argues for replacing intuition with linear models; K&T argue for correcting intuition

## Contradictions or Tensions

- Kahneman and Tversky's approach here is more conciliatory toward intuitive judgment than Dawes's (Ch. 28). Dawes argues for *replacing* clinical judgment with linear models; K&T argue for *correcting* intuitive predictions by integrating them with distributional data. Both approaches respect the same underlying statistical principles but differ in how much they trust the human component.
- The five-step procedure requires the expert to assess predictability (Step 4), which is itself subject to bias (hindsight, availability). This creates a potential circularity: the debiasing tool depends on an estimate that may itself be biased.

## Quotes Worth Keeping

> "Intuitive predictions are typically nonregressive: people often make extreme predictions on the basis of information whose reliability and predictive validity are known to be low." -- Kahneman & Tversky, Ch.30

> "The problem is not whether to accept intuitive predictions at face value or to reject them, but rather how they can be debiased and improved." -- Kahneman & Tversky, Ch.30

> "A fallible predictor can retain a chance to correctly predict a few exceptional outcomes only at the cost of erroneously identifying many other cases as exceptional." -- Kahneman & Tversky, Ch.30

relatedSummaries.title: Judgment in Managerial Decision Making Ch.12 — Improving Decision Making
relatedSummaries.authors: Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
**Type:** Book chapter (8th Ed, Ch.12, pp.206-230)
**Phase:** 2
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. Seven complementary strategies can correct systematic deficiencies in decision making: (1) use decision-analysis tools, (2) acquire expertise, (3) debias your judgment, (4) reason analogically, (5) take an outsider's view, (6) understand biases in others, and (7) nudge people toward wiser and more ethical decisions
2. The first three strategies aim to create broad change in intuitive responses to decision-making situations by heightening awareness of cognitive limitations and susceptibility to bias; the last four provide techniques for improving specific decisions in specific contexts
3. Linear models consistently outperform expert intuition across domains (admissions, hiring, medical diagnosis, investment) because they integrate information consistently and avoid the random noise in human judgment
4. Experience alone does not eliminate biases -- Tversky and Kahneman (1986) argue that basic judgmental biases are unlikely to self-correct because feedback is delayed, noisy, and rarely counterfactual; true expertise requires deliberate conceptual learning, not passive experience
5. Debiasing follows Lewin's three-stage change model: unfreezing (accepting that your judgment is flawed), change (learning specific bias-correction techniques like "consider the opposite"), and refreezing (internalizing new strategies through repeated practice and periodic self-audits)

## Detailed Notes

### The Moneyball Opening
The chapter opens with Billy Beane and the Oakland Athletics (1999-2002), who achieved the second-best record in Major League Baseball with one of the two smallest payrolls. Their success came from replacing biased expert intuition with statistical analysis. Baseball executives were guilty of three mistakes: (1) overgeneralizing from personal experience, (2) overweighting recent performance, and (3) trusting what they saw with their own eyes over multiyear statistical records. Thaler and Sunstein (2003) compare this to the broader tendency of personnel managers to base hiring on "gut" reactions to interviews rather than hard data.

### Strategy 1: Use Decision-Analysis Tools
**Core idea:** When decision quality really matters, rely on formal procedures rather than intuition. Decision analysis uses expected-value logic -- multiply an option's value by its probability to compute expected value.

**Linear models** are formulas that weight and add relevant predictor variables. They consistently outperform expert judgment across domains because:
- People are good at **selecting** and **coding** information but poor at **integrating** it (Dawes, 1979)
- Human judgment is inconsistent -- affected by mood, deadlines, random fluctuations -- while a linear model always produces the same output from the same inputs
- Experts are subject to biases triggered by specific cases; linear models use only empirically validated data

**Key evidence:**
- Einhorn (1972): Physicians coding biopsies of Hodgkin's disease made accurate individual ratings but could not predict survival time; a multiple regression model using their own selected variables could
- Dawes (1971): A linear model for graduate admissions using GRE scores, GPA, and school quality could rule out 55% of the applicant pool without rejecting anyone the committee accepted, and was better than the committee at predicting future faculty ratings
- Employment interviews predict only about 14% of variability in job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998), yet managers resist replacing them due to a "perfect storm" of availability, representativeness, and confirmation-heuristic biases

**Resistance to linear models** comes from: (1) ethical objections ("reducing people to numbers"), (2) the belief that intuition and "gut feelings" capture information models cannot, and (3) organizational inertia (what will people do when computers make the decisions?). In practice, people play a crucial role in choosing variables, setting weights, and monitoring model performance.

**Applications to admissions and hiring:**
- Graduate schools with lenient grading practices produce inflated GPAs that admissions committees mistake for high performance -- the fundamental-attribution-error (correspondence bias) at work; a linear model easily corrects for grading differences
- Structured interviews (same questions, same order, same interviewers) outperform unstructured ones at lower cost

### Strategy 2: Acquire Expertise
**Core question:** Does experience eliminate biases?

**The pessimistic view:** Tversky and Kahneman (1986) argue that learning requires accurate and immediate feedback, which is rarely available because: (i) outcomes are delayed and hard to attribute, (ii) environmental variability degrades feedback, (iii) counterfactual information is absent, and (iv) most important decisions are unique. Even when accurate feedback is available, we anchor to current states and misremember our prior predictions (Meyvis, Ratner, & Levav, 2010).

**The Acquiring a Company experiment:** Ball, Bazerman, and Carroll (1991) gave MBA participants 20 trials with full feedback and real money at stake. Across all 20 trials, there was no obvious learning trend -- only 5 of 72 participants learned. Bereby-Meyer and Grosskopf (2008) found that even hundreds of trials do not solve it.

**Experience vs. expertise distinction (Neale & Northcraft, 1989):** Experience is merely repeated feedback. Expertise requires a "strategic conceptualization" of rational decision-making -- understanding the biases that limit rationality. Northcraft and Neale (1987) showed real-estate agents were just as biased by anchoring-and-adjustment as undergraduate students, yet denied it.

**The key lesson:** Expertise requires much more than unclear, uncontrollable, and often delayed feedback. It demands constant monitoring and awareness of decision-making processes. Experience without expertise is not transferable and can even be dangerous in new contexts.

**Confucius quoted:** "By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; Second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest."

### Strategy 3: Debias Your Judgment
**Fischhoff (1982) four debiasing steps:** (1) offer warnings about the possibility of bias, (2) describe the direction of the bias, (3) provide a dose of feedback, (4) offer extended training with feedback, coaching, and whatever else it takes.

**Larrick (2004) review:** Most successful debiasing-strategies tend to be context- and bias-specific; training and testing must be closely linked and occur in close time proximity. "Consider the opposite" reduces overconfidence-in-calibration, confirmation-heuristic, and anchoring-and-adjustment effects. Groups, training in statistical reasoning, and accountability (Lerner & Tetlock, 1999) also help.

**The three-stage Lewinian model applied to debiasing:**

1. **Unfreezing** -- Breaking through resistance to change. Three forces resist unfreezing: (a) intuitive strategies have been relied on for years, (b) successful people have received positive reinforcement for past decisions, (c) balance theory (Heider, 1958) makes "there is something wrong with my decision-making" clash with "I am a successful professional." The book's quiz-and-feedback format is designed specifically to unfreeze.

2. **Change** -- Three critical steps: (a) clarify the specific deficiency, (b) explain the roots of the bias (the underlying heuristic), (c) reassure that these deficiencies are universal and do not imply poor decision-making character. The most general-purpose technique is **"consider the opposite"** (Lord, Lepper, & Preston, 1984): play devil's advocate with yourself and think about why your tentative conclusion could be wrong. Baron (1994) offers two specific sub-strategies: (i) ask "how likely is a yes answer if my hypothesis is false?" and (ii) think of alternative hypotheses and choose the test most likely to distinguish them.

3. **Refreezing** -- New strategies must develop into intuitive habits through repeated application. Schedule routine "checkups" to evaluate recent important decisions. Without frequent reinforcement, old biases return.

### Strategy 4: Reason Analogically
**Core finding:** People learn far more from cases, simulations, and real-world experiences when they abstract the underlying principle rather than focusing on surface features.

**Thompson, Gentner, Loewenstein, & Thompson research:** Participants who compared two analogous problems (e.g., learning to overcome the preference-reversal of negotiation following a house purchase and a workplace negotiation) created more generalizable insight than those who analyzed a single case. When you compare, you focus on structural similarities and form an abstract schema that transfers to new contexts.

**Idson et al. (2004):** Training based on differences (not just similarities) between related problems can reduce bias even in the notoriously resistant "Acquiring a Company" problem. Comparing the Monty Hall problem's two versions and the Dividing a Pie problem's two versions as pairs helped participants generalize the importance of focusing on the other party's decisions and the rules of the game.

**Moran, Bereby-Meyer, and Bazerman (2008):** More diverse analogical training -- comparing two cases that illustrate different value-creating strategies (e.g., logrolling and compatibility) -- fosters greater learning of general principles than specific training on a single strategy. However, if training becomes too diverse, the applicability of the message may be lost.

### Strategy 5: Take an Outsider's View
**Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) insider/outsider distinction:**
- The **insider** is the biased decision maker who views each situation as unique
- The **outsider** generalizes across situations and identifies patterns

The insider view leads to systematic overestimation because optimism and overconfidence-in-calibration combine with the human tendency to view each decision as unique, overlooking historical base rates.

**Key examples:**
- Kahneman's own curriculum team estimated 18-30 months; a team member revealed that 40% of comparable projects were never completed and none finished in less than seven years. The project took eight years.
- Cooper, Woo, and Dunkelberg (1988): 80%+ of entrepreneurs perceived their success probability at 70% or better, one-third considered success certain. Meanwhile, the five-year survival rate for new businesses is only about 33%.
- People predict their friends' home renovations will go 20-50% over budget (outsider view) while believing their own project will finish on time (insider view).

**Practical advice:** For decisions that really matter, ask friends or colleagues with relevant experience for their honest estimate. Or imagine the decision is a friend's and ask what advice you would give. The key is to give the outsider a stronger voice.

### Strategy 6: Understand Biases in Others
**Core shift:** Auditing others' decisions, not just your own. The same biases operate in everyone, but detecting them in others requires a different analytical stance.

**Site-location analyst example:** A retail chain's analyst predicts $3.8M in annual sales for a new store. The mean of all stores is $3M. The director should adjust the prediction toward the mean, proportionally based on the analyst's historical accuracy (the correlation between her predictions and actual sales). If correlation = 0.5, the adjusted estimate is $3.4M. If correlation = 0, the best estimate is simply the mean ($3M).

**Kahneman and Tversky (1982) five-step corrective process:**
1. Select a comparison group
2. Assess the distribution of the comparison group
3. Incorporate intuitive estimation (identify the initial forecast)
4. Assess the predicted results of the decision (determine the correlation between forecast and reality)
5. Adjust the intuitive estimate using the formula: adjusted estimate = group mean + correlation x (initial estimate - group mean)

**Three-phase model for adjusting biased decisions in others:**
1. Accurately perceive the context in which the decision is being made
2. Distinguish the potential bias(es) surrounding the decision and the decision makers
3. Identify and make the appropriate logical adjustments

**Competitive application:** Richard Thaler and Russell Fuller created the Fuller-Thaler mutual funds, which buy securities by exploiting the predictable biases of other market participants -- e.g., most analysts underreact to new positive information about firms, creating temporary undervaluation.

### Strategy 7: Nudge Wiser and More Ethical Decisions
**Thaler and Sunstein (2008) -- "libertarian paternalism":** Design choice architectures that nudge people toward better decisions while preserving freedom of choice.

**Organ donation example:** Most Americans prefer option (a) -- heart used to save a life, with 90% chance of receiving one if needed. Yet U.S. policy resembles option (b) -- buried with heart, 45% chance. Why? Loss-aversion makes opt-out feel like losing something. European countries with opt-out programs have organ donation rates of 86-100% vs. 4-28% for opt-in countries.

**Save More Tomorrow (Thaler & Benartzi, 2004):** Workers commit in advance to increase 401(k) contributions when they get future raises. Leverages hyperbolic-discounting (easier to commit to future sacrifice), inertia/status quo bias (people rarely opt out once enrolled), and loss-aversion (savings increase comes from new income, not current take-home). Result: more than tripled savings rates in just over two years. 39% of large U.S. employers had adopted it by 2007.

**Nudging hiring decisions (Bohnet, van Geen, & Bazerman, 2012):** When evaluating candidates one at a time, people rely on gender stereotypes (men for math, women for verbal). When two or more candidates are evaluated jointly, decision makers shift to focusing on individual capabilities, producing both more ethical and more meritocratic hiring.

### Conclusion
The first three strategies seek broad change in intuitive responses; the last four provide techniques for improving specific decisions in specific contexts. Together, they provide tools for changing and "refreezing" intuitive decision-making processes.

The responsibility for refreezing lies with the reader. Lasting improvement requires persistent monitoring and vigilance across the complex world of decisions. It is far easier to identify a bias while reading a book than when in the midst of an organizational crisis. Raiffa (1984) found that his students applied decision-making strategies on exams but failed to generalize to courses taught by other instructors.

In addition to improving your own decisions, the ideas should inform you about the decisions of others -- reporters, politicians, and other information providers constantly exemplify biased processes.

The authors conclude: managers tend to reward results rather than good decision processes. Because decisions involve uncertainty, good decisions sometimes turn out badly and bad decisions sometimes turn out well. To the extent that a manager rewards results and not sound decision making, the manager rewards behaviors that may not work in the future.

## New Entities Introduced
- entities/books/moneyball (Lewis, 2003) -- story of statistical decision-making replacing biased intuition in baseball
- entities/books/nudge (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008) -- libertarian paternalism and choice architecture

## New Concepts Introduced
- debiasing-strategies -- the seven-strategy framework for improving decision making
- Lewinian change model applied to debiasing (unfreeze-change-refreeze)

## Contradictions or Tensions
- **Expertise vs. experience:** Neale and Northcraft (1989) distinguish these sharply -- experience (passive feedback) may actually increase overconfidence-in-calibration, while expertise (strategic conceptualization) can reduce bias. This challenges the folk intuition that "more experience = better judgment."
- **Disclosure as cure for self-serving-bias-in-decisions:** Cain, Loewenstein, and Moore (2005) (from Ch.8) showed disclosure can actually increase bias by giving advisers moral license. The current chapter's Strategy 7 (nudging) provides a structural alternative to mere disclosure.
- **Individual debiasing vs. systemic nudges:** The chapter implicitly acknowledges tension between Strategies 1-5 (individual improvement) and Strategy 7 (system design). Fischhoff and Larrick both note that individual debiasing has limited durability without systemic support.

## Quotes Worth Keeping
> "By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; Second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest." — Confucius, quoted via Dawes (1988), p.217

> "The folks who run mutual funds have always been good at cooking up clever ways to gouge you on fees, confuse you about performance, make you pay unnecessary taxes and goad you into buying funds you don't need." — Jason Zweig (2000), via Bazerman & Moore, p.162

> "Learning from an experience of failure . . . is indeed 'dear,' and it can even be fatal. . . . moreover, experiences of success may have negative as well as positive results when people mindlessly learn from them. . . . People who are extraordinarily successful -- or lucky -- in general may conclude from their 'experience' that they are invulnerable and consequently court disaster by failing to monitor their behavior and its implications." — Dawes (1988), p.216

relatedSummaries.title: Never Split the Difference Ch.6: Bend Their Reality — Summary
relatedSummaries.source: 5-20 - Never Split the Difference - Voss, Raz
relatedSummaries.content:
**Authors:** chris-voss, tahl-raz
**Source:** *5-20 - Never Split the Difference - Voss, Raz*, Chapter 6
**Phase:** 5 — Negotiation
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-15

## Key Takeaways

1. **Never split the difference** — compromise is often the worst outcome. A woman wants black shoes, her husband wants brown shoes; they compromise and he wears one of each. Both lose. Creative solutions beat lazy compromises.
2. **Deadlines are mostly imaginary** and almost never carry the consequences people fear. The mantra: "No deal is better than a bad deal." Hiding deadlines increases impasse risk (Don A. Moore, UC Berkeley).
3. **The F-word ("Fair") is the most powerful word in negotiation** — it triggers deep emotional responses rooted in the insular cortex. There are three ways people use it, and only one is constructive: proactively establishing that you want things to be fair at the outset.
4. **Bend reality by anchoring extreme** — before making your "real" offer, emotionally anchor with how bad things will be, then present your number as a relative relief. The anchoring-and-adjustment effect makes this devastatingly effective.
5. **People take more risks to avoid losses than to realize gains** — loss-aversion from prospect-theory means you must frame what your counterpart stands to lose by inaction.
6. **Use odd, precise numbers** — $37,263 feels calculated and immovable; $38,000 feels like a placeholder. Precision signals thoughtful analysis.

## Detailed Notes

### Don't Compromise

The core thesis of the book: never split the difference. Compromise is a lazy substitute for creative problem-solving. In negotiation, we are taught to seek "win-win," but the win-win mindset pushed by many experts is usually ineffective and often disastrous. It satisfies neither side. "We don't compromise because it's right; we compromise because it is easy and because it saves face."

Most people in a negotiation are driven by fear or by the desire to avoid pain. Too few are driven by their actual goals. Creative solutions are almost always preceded by some degree of risk, annoyance, confusion, and conflict.

### Deadlines: Make Time Your Ally — deadline-pressure

- Time and deadlines are the screw that pressures every deal to a conclusion
- Deadlines regularly make people say and do impulsive things against their best interests
- Good negotiators resist the urge to rush and take advantage of it in others
- **Deadlines are the bogeymen of negotiation** — almost exclusively self-inflicted figments of our imagination
- Voss asked nearly every entrepreneur and executive he worked with whether a missed deadline had ever had negative repercussions. Among hundreds, exactly one answered yes.
- **Herb Cohen's Japan story**: Cohen told his Japanese counterparts he was staying a week. They entertained him for seven days and only started serious talks as he was leaving for the airport. Hiding his deadline hurt him — "They knew my deadline, but I didn't know theirs."
- **Don A. Moore (Haas School of Business, Berkeley)**: Hiding deadlines dramatically increases the risk of impasse. Revealing your deadline actually gets better deals — it reduces impasse risk and speeds concession-making.
- **Deadlines cut both ways** — when negotiation is over for one side, it's over for the other side too
- **Haitian kidnapping patterns**: Kidnappers wanted to get paid by Friday to party on the weekend. By stalling until Thursday or Friday, Voss's team cut the best deals. Increasing specificity in threats indicated proximity to a real deadline (What? Who? When? How?).

### No Such Thing as Fair — fairness-in-negotiation

- **The Ultimatum Game**: Students split $10 between a "proposer" and "accepter." No one converges on the same split. All reasoning is "100 percent irrational and emotional."
- Accepters invariably reject offers below half. Below a quarter, they become insulted. The negative emotional value of unfairness outweighs the positive rational value of the money.
