- **Standard economics vs. fairness constraints:** The paper directly challenges the assumption that firms set prices solely by supply and demand. Fairness acts as a friction that prevents market clearing, contradicts perfect price discrimination, and produces asymmetric price rigidity.
- **Self-interest vs. intrinsic fairness:** The evidence on tipping and mechanic scenarios suggests firms and individuals sometimes act fairly even when enforcement is impossible, challenging the pure self-interest assumption.
- **Cost-plus rule vs. dual entitlement:** The data reject a simple cost-plus rule of fair pricing. Firms are not required to pass on cost decreases to consumers, creating an asymmetry between cost increases (must be absorbed or passed through proportionally) and cost decreases (may be retained).

## Cross-References

- loss-aversion — The asymmetry between losses and gains in fairness judgments is a direct manifestation of loss aversion applied to social evaluation
- reference-dependence — Fairness judgments are entirely reference-dependent; the reference transaction anchors all evaluations
- endowment-effect — Transactors' entitlement to reference terms parallels the endowment effect; what you have (your current wage, your current price) feels like it is yours
- ultimatum-game — Key evidence for willingness to punish unfairness at personal cost
- prospect-theory — The theoretical foundation; fairness judgments follow the same gain/loss asymmetries documented in prospect theory
- framing-effects — Firms can exploit framing (discounts vs. surcharges, bonuses vs. base wages) to make identical economic actions appear more or less fair

## Quotes Worth Keeping

> "A hardware store has been selling snow shovels for $15. The morning after a large snowstorm, the store raises the price to $20. ... 82 percent of respondents (N = 107) considered it unfair for the hardware store to take advantage of the short-run increase in demand associated with a blizzard." — Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler, Question 1

> "The main findings of this research can be summarized by a principle of dual entitlement, which governs community standards of fairness: Transactors have an entitlement to the terms of the reference transaction and firms are entitled to their reference profit." — Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler

> "The cardinal rule of fair behavior is surely that one person should not achieve a gain by simply imposing an equivalent loss on another." — Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler

> "It is a mild embarrassment to the standard model that experimental studies often produce fair behavior even in the absence of enforcement." — Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler

> "Judgments of fairness are also susceptible to framing effects, in which form appears to overwhelm substance." — Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler

skills.title: Overconfidence
skills.subtitle: You're less right than you think you are -- and you're sure about that
skills.challenge: Make 10 predictions this week (project timelines, meeting outcomes, quiz answers) and assign confidence percentages. At the end of the week, score yourself. Your calibration gap is the difference between your average confidence and your actual accuracy.
skills.definition: Overconfidence in calibration is the tendency for people's subjective confidence in their judgments to systematically exceed their objective accuracy. When people say they are 90% sure of something, they are typically correct only about 70-80% of the time. This miscalibration leads to insufficient consideration of alternatives and inadequate preparation for uncertainty.
skills.content:
## Definition

Overconfidence in calibration is the systematic tendency to set **confidence intervals that are far too narrow** — people believe they know more precisely than they actually do. When asked for ranges they are 98% sure contain the true value, the true value falls outside those ranges roughly 30% of the time.

## Key Findings

- Subjects asked to estimate quantities (e.g., the Dow-Jones average, lengths of rivers) and provide 1st/99th percentile bounds consistently set ranges too narrow (summary-1-01-judgment-under-uncertainty)
- The error rate was ~30% instead of the expected 2% — a 15x calibration failure
- Two procedures were tested (setting extremes first vs. starting from a best estimate); both showed severe overconfidence
- This is distinct from overconfidence in accuracy (believing your point estimate is correct); calibration overconfidence is about the precision of your uncertainty

## Mechanisms

The anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic drives calibration overconfidence. When setting a confidence range, people start from their best estimate (the anchor) and adjust outward to set the bounds. But the adjustment is insufficient — they don't move far enough from the anchor. The result: ranges that are too centered on the point estimate, too narrow, and that exclude the true value far more often than they should.

## Applications

- **Project planning:** Time and cost estimates with "worst case" bounds that are routinely exceeded
- **Financial forecasting:** Analysts whose prediction ranges fail to capture actual outcomes
- **Strategic planning:** Business plans that underestimate the range of possible outcomes
- **Risk management:** Confidence intervals around risk estimates that are far too tight
- **Negotiation:** Overconfidence in one's assessment of BATNA or the other party's reservation price

## Bazerman & Moore Extensions

Bazerman and Moore (summary-2-08-bazerman-ch2) massively extend this concept by placing it within a three-part taxonomy of overconfidence:

- **Overprecision** (overprecision) is the formal name for calibration overconfidence -- the most robust form of overconfidence
- **Overestimation** (overestimation) -- thinking we are better than we actually are (self-enhancement, illusion of control, planning fallacy, optimistic biases)
- **Overplacement** (overplacement) -- thinking we are better than others (better-than-average effect, Lake Wobegon effect)
- Overconfidence is called "the mother of all biases" -- the most potent, pervasive, and pernicious (Griffin & Varey, 1996), blamed for wars, stock bubbles, bankruptcy, Chernobyl, the Challenger explosion, and the subprime crisis
- Overconfidence facilitates all other biases: if we were appropriately humble, we could more easily double-check and correct our flaws
- **Key new evidence:** Financial officers' 80% confidence intervals captured actual returns only 33% of the time (Ben-David, Graham, & Harvey, 2010); scientists' confidence intervals for physical constants were too narrow (Henrion & Fischhoff, 1986); experts in their own domains were equally overprecise (McKenzie, Liersch, & Yaniv, 2008)
- The prescription: strive for well-calibrated beliefs that match reality, not positive illusions

## Fischhoff's Debiasing Review (1982)

Fischhoff (summary-2-06-hb-ch31-debiasing) exhaustively reviewed all published attempts to debias overconfidence, organized by his debiasing-taxonomy:

- **Unfair tasks:** Response-mode manipulations (probability vs. odds, fixed-value vs. fixed-probability methods) had mixed results. Raising stakes did not reliably reduce overconfidence (Sieber, 1974). Proper scoring rules are theoretically ideal but asymmetrically penalize overconfidence, potentially producing mechanical reduction without improved understanding.
- **Misunderstood tasks:** Some extreme overconfidence occurs on tasks where subjects have no knowledge; Fischhoff & Slovic (1980) found overconfidence was only partially reduced by cautioning that tasks might be impossible.
- **Perfectible individuals:** Training with personalized feedback showed promise -- one round was as effective as extended series (Lichtenstein & Fischhoff, 1980b). Key conditions: large sample feedback, performance-specific information, discussion of uncertainty-probability mapping.
- **Incorrigible individuals:** Recalibration (mechanically adjusting confidence downward) requires task-specific knowledge of the overconfidence level, making it impractical in general.
- **Restructuring (most effective):** Having respondents list reasons why their preferred answer might be wrong (Koriat, Lichtenstein, & Fischhoff, 1980) reduced overconfidence. This works because it specifically prompts searching for disconfirming evidence. Listing reasons for AND against had no effect -- the critical element is the directional prompt to "consider why you might be wrong."
- **Education:** Weather forecasters show excellent calibration due to explicit feedback rewards (Murphy & Winkler, 1974). Experts without calibration training (psychologists, bankers, engineers, executives) show overconfidence. Difficulty level is the most potent factor: overconfidence with hard questions, underconfidence with easy ones.

Overall finding: overconfidence is remarkably resistant to most interventions. Effective debiasing requires changing the psychological nature of the task, not just exhorting people to be less confident.

## Cross-References
- **Parent heuristic:** anchoring-and-adjustment
- **Related concepts:** overprecision, overestimation, overplacement, illusion-of-validity, confirmation-heuristic, debiasing-taxonomy, debiasing-strategies
- **Key authors:** tversky, kahneman, bazerman, fischhoff

relatedSummaries.title: Judgment in Managerial Decision Making Ch.12 — Improving Decision Making
relatedSummaries.authors: Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
**Type:** Book chapter (8th Ed, Ch.12, pp.206-230)
**Phase:** 2
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. Seven complementary strategies can correct systematic deficiencies in decision making: (1) use decision-analysis tools, (2) acquire expertise, (3) debias your judgment, (4) reason analogically, (5) take an outsider's view, (6) understand biases in others, and (7) nudge people toward wiser and more ethical decisions
2. The first three strategies aim to create broad change in intuitive responses to decision-making situations by heightening awareness of cognitive limitations and susceptibility to bias; the last four provide techniques for improving specific decisions in specific contexts
3. Linear models consistently outperform expert intuition across domains (admissions, hiring, medical diagnosis, investment) because they integrate information consistently and avoid the random noise in human judgment
4. Experience alone does not eliminate biases -- Tversky and Kahneman (1986) argue that basic judgmental biases are unlikely to self-correct because feedback is delayed, noisy, and rarely counterfactual; true expertise requires deliberate conceptual learning, not passive experience
5. Debiasing follows Lewin's three-stage change model: unfreezing (accepting that your judgment is flawed), change (learning specific bias-correction techniques like "consider the opposite"), and refreezing (internalizing new strategies through repeated practice and periodic self-audits)

## Detailed Notes

### The Moneyball Opening
The chapter opens with Billy Beane and the Oakland Athletics (1999-2002), who achieved the second-best record in Major League Baseball with one of the two smallest payrolls. Their success came from replacing biased expert intuition with statistical analysis. Baseball executives were guilty of three mistakes: (1) overgeneralizing from personal experience, (2) overweighting recent performance, and (3) trusting what they saw with their own eyes over multiyear statistical records. Thaler and Sunstein (2003) compare this to the broader tendency of personnel managers to base hiring on "gut" reactions to interviews rather than hard data.

### Strategy 1: Use Decision-Analysis Tools
**Core idea:** When decision quality really matters, rely on formal procedures rather than intuition. Decision analysis uses expected-value logic -- multiply an option's value by its probability to compute expected value.

**Linear models** are formulas that weight and add relevant predictor variables. They consistently outperform expert judgment across domains because:
- People are good at **selecting** and **coding** information but poor at **integrating** it (Dawes, 1979)
- Human judgment is inconsistent -- affected by mood, deadlines, random fluctuations -- while a linear model always produces the same output from the same inputs
- Experts are subject to biases triggered by specific cases; linear models use only empirically validated data

**Key evidence:**
- Einhorn (1972): Physicians coding biopsies of Hodgkin's disease made accurate individual ratings but could not predict survival time; a multiple regression model using their own selected variables could
- Dawes (1971): A linear model for graduate admissions using GRE scores, GPA, and school quality could rule out 55% of the applicant pool without rejecting anyone the committee accepted, and was better than the committee at predicting future faculty ratings
- Employment interviews predict only about 14% of variability in job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998), yet managers resist replacing them due to a "perfect storm" of availability, representativeness, and confirmation-heuristic biases

**Resistance to linear models** comes from: (1) ethical objections ("reducing people to numbers"), (2) the belief that intuition and "gut feelings" capture information models cannot, and (3) organizational inertia (what will people do when computers make the decisions?). In practice, people play a crucial role in choosing variables, setting weights, and monitoring model performance.

**Applications to admissions and hiring:**
- Graduate schools with lenient grading practices produce inflated GPAs that admissions committees mistake for high performance -- the fundamental-attribution-error (correspondence bias) at work; a linear model easily corrects for grading differences
- Structured interviews (same questions, same order, same interviewers) outperform unstructured ones at lower cost

### Strategy 2: Acquire Expertise
**Core question:** Does experience eliminate biases?

**The pessimistic view:** Tversky and Kahneman (1986) argue that learning requires accurate and immediate feedback, which is rarely available because: (i) outcomes are delayed and hard to attribute, (ii) environmental variability degrades feedback, (iii) counterfactual information is absent, and (iv) most important decisions are unique. Even when accurate feedback is available, we anchor to current states and misremember our prior predictions (Meyvis, Ratner, & Levav, 2010).

**The Acquiring a Company experiment:** Ball, Bazerman, and Carroll (1991) gave MBA participants 20 trials with full feedback and real money at stake. Across all 20 trials, there was no obvious learning trend -- only 5 of 72 participants learned. Bereby-Meyer and Grosskopf (2008) found that even hundreds of trials do not solve it.

**Experience vs. expertise distinction (Neale & Northcraft, 1989):** Experience is merely repeated feedback. Expertise requires a "strategic conceptualization" of rational decision-making -- understanding the biases that limit rationality. Northcraft and Neale (1987) showed real-estate agents were just as biased by anchoring-and-adjustment as undergraduate students, yet denied it.

**The key lesson:** Expertise requires much more than unclear, uncontrollable, and often delayed feedback. It demands constant monitoring and awareness of decision-making processes. Experience without expertise is not transferable and can even be dangerous in new contexts.

**Confucius quoted:** "By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; Second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest."

### Strategy 3: Debias Your Judgment
**Fischhoff (1982) four debiasing steps:** (1) offer warnings about the possibility of bias, (2) describe the direction of the bias, (3) provide a dose of feedback, (4) offer extended training with feedback, coaching, and whatever else it takes.

**Larrick (2004) review:** Most successful debiasing-strategies tend to be context- and bias-specific; training and testing must be closely linked and occur in close time proximity. "Consider the opposite" reduces overconfidence-in-calibration, confirmation-heuristic, and anchoring-and-adjustment effects. Groups, training in statistical reasoning, and accountability (Lerner & Tetlock, 1999) also help.

**The three-stage Lewinian model applied to debiasing:**

1. **Unfreezing** -- Breaking through resistance to change. Three forces resist unfreezing: (a) intuitive strategies have been relied on for years, (b) successful people have received positive reinforcement for past decisions, (c) balance theory (Heider, 1958) makes "there is something wrong with my decision-making" clash with "I am a successful professional." The book's quiz-and-feedback format is designed specifically to unfreeze.

2. **Change** -- Three critical steps: (a) clarify the specific deficiency, (b) explain the roots of the bias (the underlying heuristic), (c) reassure that these deficiencies are universal and do not imply poor decision-making character. The most general-purpose technique is **"consider the opposite"** (Lord, Lepper, & Preston, 1984): play devil's advocate with yourself and think about why your tentative conclusion could be wrong. Baron (1994) offers two specific sub-strategies: (i) ask "how likely is a yes answer if my hypothesis is false?" and (ii) think of alternative hypotheses and choose the test most likely to distinguish them.

3. **Refreezing** -- New strategies must develop into intuitive habits through repeated application. Schedule routine "checkups" to evaluate recent important decisions. Without frequent reinforcement, old biases return.

### Strategy 4: Reason Analogically
**Core finding:** People learn far more from cases, simulations, and real-world experiences when they abstract the underlying principle rather than focusing on surface features.

**Thompson, Gentner, Loewenstein, & Thompson research:** Participants who compared two analogous problems (e.g., learning to overcome the preference-reversal of negotiation following a house purchase and a workplace negotiation) created more generalizable insight than those who analyzed a single case. When you compare, you focus on structural similarities and form an abstract schema that transfers to new contexts.

**Idson et al. (2004):** Training based on differences (not just similarities) between related problems can reduce bias even in the notoriously resistant "Acquiring a Company" problem. Comparing the Monty Hall problem's two versions and the Dividing a Pie problem's two versions as pairs helped participants generalize the importance of focusing on the other party's decisions and the rules of the game.

**Moran, Bereby-Meyer, and Bazerman (2008):** More diverse analogical training -- comparing two cases that illustrate different value-creating strategies (e.g., logrolling and compatibility) -- fosters greater learning of general principles than specific training on a single strategy. However, if training becomes too diverse, the applicability of the message may be lost.

### Strategy 5: Take an Outsider's View
**Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) insider/outsider distinction:**
- The **insider** is the biased decision maker who views each situation as unique
- The **outsider** generalizes across situations and identifies patterns

The insider view leads to systematic overestimation because optimism and overconfidence-in-calibration combine with the human tendency to view each decision as unique, overlooking historical base rates.

**Key examples:**
- Kahneman's own curriculum team estimated 18-30 months; a team member revealed that 40% of comparable projects were never completed and none finished in less than seven years. The project took eight years.
- Cooper, Woo, and Dunkelberg (1988): 80%+ of entrepreneurs perceived their success probability at 70% or better, one-third considered success certain. Meanwhile, the five-year survival rate for new businesses is only about 33%.
- People predict their friends' home renovations will go 20-50% over budget (outsider view) while believing their own project will finish on time (insider view).

**Practical advice:** For decisions that really matter, ask friends or colleagues with relevant experience for their honest estimate. Or imagine the decision is a friend's and ask what advice you would give. The key is to give the outsider a stronger voice.

### Strategy 6: Understand Biases in Others
**Core shift:** Auditing others' decisions, not just your own. The same biases operate in everyone, but detecting them in others requires a different analytical stance.

**Site-location analyst example:** A retail chain's analyst predicts $3.8M in annual sales for a new store. The mean of all stores is $3M. The director should adjust the prediction toward the mean, proportionally based on the analyst's historical accuracy (the correlation between her predictions and actual sales). If correlation = 0.5, the adjusted estimate is $3.4M. If correlation = 0, the best estimate is simply the mean ($3M).

**Kahneman and Tversky (1982) five-step corrective process:**
1. Select a comparison group
2. Assess the distribution of the comparison group
3. Incorporate intuitive estimation (identify the initial forecast)
4. Assess the predicted results of the decision (determine the correlation between forecast and reality)
5. Adjust the intuitive estimate using the formula: adjusted estimate = group mean + correlation x (initial estimate - group mean)

**Three-phase model for adjusting biased decisions in others:**
1. Accurately perceive the context in which the decision is being made
2. Distinguish the potential bias(es) surrounding the decision and the decision makers
3. Identify and make the appropriate logical adjustments

**Competitive application:** Richard Thaler and Russell Fuller created the Fuller-Thaler mutual funds, which buy securities by exploiting the predictable biases of other market participants -- e.g., most analysts underreact to new positive information about firms, creating temporary undervaluation.

### Strategy 7: Nudge Wiser and More Ethical Decisions
**Thaler and Sunstein (2008) -- "libertarian paternalism":** Design choice architectures that nudge people toward better decisions while preserving freedom of choice.

**Organ donation example:** Most Americans prefer option (a) -- heart used to save a life, with 90% chance of receiving one if needed. Yet U.S. policy resembles option (b) -- buried with heart, 45% chance. Why? Loss-aversion makes opt-out feel like losing something. European countries with opt-out programs have organ donation rates of 86-100% vs. 4-28% for opt-in countries.

**Save More Tomorrow (Thaler & Benartzi, 2004):** Workers commit in advance to increase 401(k) contributions when they get future raises. Leverages hyperbolic-discounting (easier to commit to future sacrifice), inertia/status quo bias (people rarely opt out once enrolled), and loss-aversion (savings increase comes from new income, not current take-home). Result: more than tripled savings rates in just over two years. 39% of large U.S. employers had adopted it by 2007.

**Nudging hiring decisions (Bohnet, van Geen, & Bazerman, 2012):** When evaluating candidates one at a time, people rely on gender stereotypes (men for math, women for verbal). When two or more candidates are evaluated jointly, decision makers shift to focusing on individual capabilities, producing both more ethical and more meritocratic hiring.

### Conclusion
The first three strategies seek broad change in intuitive responses; the last four provide techniques for improving specific decisions in specific contexts. Together, they provide tools for changing and "refreezing" intuitive decision-making processes.

The responsibility for refreezing lies with the reader. Lasting improvement requires persistent monitoring and vigilance across the complex world of decisions. It is far easier to identify a bias while reading a book than when in the midst of an organizational crisis. Raiffa (1984) found that his students applied decision-making strategies on exams but failed to generalize to courses taught by other instructors.

In addition to improving your own decisions, the ideas should inform you about the decisions of others -- reporters, politicians, and other information providers constantly exemplify biased processes.

The authors conclude: managers tend to reward results rather than good decision processes. Because decisions involve uncertainty, good decisions sometimes turn out badly and bad decisions sometimes turn out well. To the extent that a manager rewards results and not sound decision making, the manager rewards behaviors that may not work in the future.

## New Entities Introduced
- entities/books/moneyball (Lewis, 2003) -- story of statistical decision-making replacing biased intuition in baseball
- entities/books/nudge (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008) -- libertarian paternalism and choice architecture

## New Concepts Introduced
- debiasing-strategies -- the seven-strategy framework for improving decision making
- Lewinian change model applied to debiasing (unfreeze-change-refreeze)

## Contradictions or Tensions
- **Expertise vs. experience:** Neale and Northcraft (1989) distinguish these sharply -- experience (passive feedback) may actually increase overconfidence-in-calibration, while expertise (strategic conceptualization) can reduce bias. This challenges the folk intuition that "more experience = better judgment."
- **Disclosure as cure for self-serving-bias-in-decisions:** Cain, Loewenstein, and Moore (2005) (from Ch.8) showed disclosure can actually increase bias by giving advisers moral license. The current chapter's Strategy 7 (nudging) provides a structural alternative to mere disclosure.
- **Individual debiasing vs. systemic nudges:** The chapter implicitly acknowledges tension between Strategies 1-5 (individual improvement) and Strategy 7 (system design). Fischhoff and Larrick both note that individual debiasing has limited durability without systemic support.

## Quotes Worth Keeping
> "By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; Second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest." — Confucius, quoted via Dawes (1988), p.217

> "The folks who run mutual funds have always been good at cooking up clever ways to gouge you on fees, confuse you about performance, make you pay unnecessary taxes and goad you into buying funds you don't need." — Jason Zweig (2000), via Bazerman & Moore, p.162

> "Learning from an experience of failure . . . is indeed 'dear,' and it can even be fatal. . . . moreover, experiences of success may have negative as well as positive results when people mindlessly learn from them. . . . People who are extraordinarily successful -- or lucky -- in general may conclude from their 'experience' that they are invulnerable and consequently court disaster by failing to monitor their behavior and its implications." — Dawes (1988), p.216

relatedSummaries.title: The Illusion of Control — Summary
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Ellen J. Langer
**Type:** Research paper (Chapter 16 in *Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases*)
**Published:** 1982, in Kahneman, Slovic, & Tversky (Eds.), Cambridge University Press
**Phase:** 2 — Decision Science
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. People routinely behave as though they can influence outcomes that are entirely determined by chance. Langer defines the **illusion of control** as "an expectancy of a personal success probability inappropriately higher than the objective probability would warrant."
2. The illusion is triggered by introducing **skill-related cues** into chance settings: competition, choice, stimulus familiarity, and active involvement.
3. Even in situations as transparently chance-driven as lotteries and card games, these cues cause people to behave as if outcomes are controllable -- betting more against weak opponents, valuing self-chosen tickets far above randomly assigned ones.
4. The effect arises from two sources: (a) a deep motivation to master one's environment, and (b) genuine difficulty discriminating skill from chance because the two are intertwined in everyday experience.

## Detailed Notes

### The Central Thesis

Langer argues that the distinction between skill and chance, while clear in principle, is not recognized in practice. In skill situations, there is a causal link between behavior and outcome; in chance situations, there is not. But people treat chance events as controllable whenever the situation mimics features of skill contexts.

### Experiment 1: Competition (Dapper vs. Schnook)

36 Yale undergraduates played a card-drawing game (pure chance -- whoever draws the higher card wins). The opponent was a confederate who appeared either confident and well-dressed ("dapper") or nervous and awkward ("schnook").

**Results:** Subjects bet significantly more against the schnook (mean bet 16.25 cents) than against the dapper confederate (11.04 cents), t = 2.39, p < .025. First-round bets showed an even larger gap (16.72 cents vs. 9.28 cents, t = 3.16, p < .005).

**Interpretation:** In a pure chance game, the opponent's apparent competence should be irrelevant. Subjects' behavior makes sense only if they unconsciously treated the card game as a skill contest where beating a weaker opponent is easier.

### Experiment 2: Choice (Lottery Ticket Valuation)

Office workers in a lottery ($1 ticket, ~$50 pot) were randomly assigned to choose their own football-card ticket or receive one assigned to them. On the morning of the drawing, each was asked how much they would sell the ticket for.

**Results:** Choosers demanded $8.67 on average; non-choosers asked for only $1.96, t = 4.33, p < .005. Ten of 15 people who initially refused to sell were in the choice condition. The act of choosing -- a skill-related behavior -- inflated the perceived value of a lottery ticket by more than 4x.

**Ancillary finding on familiarity:** Females, less familiar with football, demanded far less ($1.33 mean vs. $5.89 for males). Four of the four people who refused to enter the lottery at all were female, suggesting familiarity with the stimulus domain strengthens the illusion.

### Additional Skill-Related Factors

The paper describes competition, choice, stimulus familiarity, response familiarity, and active involvement as the key cues that trigger skill-oriented processing in chance contexts. The logic: these are all features people associate with skill settings. When they appear in chance settings, they activate skill-oriented cognition, and with it the expectation of personal control.

### Why It Happens

Langer identifies two complementary explanations:

1. **Motivation to control:** A fundamental human drive variously labeled as need for competence (White), instinct to master (Hendrick), striving for superiority (Adler), or striving for personal causation (deCharms). The ultimate expression of mastery would be controlling the uncontrollable.
2. **Genuine difficulty discriminating:** Skill and chance are deeply intertwined in real experience. Every skill situation has chance elements (lucky breaks), and every chance situation has skill-like features (knowing the odds, choosing when to bet). The boundary is genuinely blurry, making misclassification natural.

### Observational Evidence

- **Casino dealers** who experience runs of bad luck risk being fired -- as if they are causing the losses.
- **Dice players** throw softly for low numbers and hard for high numbers, behave as if effort and concentration affect random outcomes, and choose to bet with the player who "looks like he has the most control."
- **Pre-outcome vs. post-outcome betting:** Strickland, Lewicki, & Katz (1966) found subjects bet more when wagering *before* the dice toss than after (but before the outcome is revealed) -- consistent with believing one can influence the toss.

## New Entities Introduced

- langer -- Ellen J. Langer, social psychologist, Yale / Harvard

## New Concepts Introduced

- illusion-of-control -- Expecting personal success probability higher than objective probability warrants, triggered by skill-related cues in chance situations

## Contradictions or Tensions

- The illusion of control is related to but distinct from overconfidence-in-calibration and overestimation. Overconfidence concerns the precision of knowledge estimates; the illusion of control concerns the misattribution of causal influence over outcomes. Bazerman & Moore (summary-2-08-bazerman-ch2) list the illusion of control as one of the biases stemming from overconfidence-in-calibration, but Langer's original formulation emphasizes skill-chance confusion rather than calibration per se.
- The motivation-to-control explanation connects to the need for competence and autonomy as fundamental human drives, a theme that will recur in Phase 3 motivation science.

## Quotes Worth Keeping

> "An illusion of control is defined as an expectancy of a personal success probability inappropriately higher than the objective probability would warrant." — Langer, p. 231

> "The greatest satisfaction or feeling of competence would therefore result from being able to control the seemingly uncontrollable." — Langer, p. 237

> "There is not only a motivation not to discriminate, but there is often a true difficulty in making the discrimination, since there is an element of chance in every skill situation and an element of skill in almost every chance situation." — Langer, p. 238

relatedSummaries.title: Judgment in Managerial Decision Making Ch.9 — Common Investment Mistakes
relatedSummaries.authors: Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
**Type:** Book chapter (8th Ed, Ch.9, pp.159-175)
**Phase:** 2
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. Index funds consistently outperform the vast majority of actively managed mutual funds and hedge funds, yet most investors persist in paying high fees for active management due to overconfidence-in-calibration and optimism bias
2. Five core biases systematically distort investment decisions: overconfidence, optimism, denial of randomness, anchoring/status quo/procrastination, and prospect theory effects (selling winners too early, holding losers too long)
3. The "disposition effect" -- investors sell winning stocks too early (locking in gains) and hold losing stocks too long (avoiding booking losses) -- is a direct consequence of prospect-theory and loss-aversion
4. Daytrading is a particularly destructive form of overconfidence: the typical daytrader underperforms the market by 3+ percentage points and faces catastrophic personal financial consequences
5. The single most actionable piece of investment advice from behavioral finance: formulate a long-term asset allocation plan, invest in low-cost index funds, and stop paying attention to the market

## Detailed Notes

### Why Active Management Fails

The Vanguard Index 500 fund has outperformed about 75% of actively managed mutual funds each year. The reason is straightforward:
- Active fund fees are often 2% annually vs. 0.2% for index funds
- Active funds have higher brokerage costs from frequent trading
- The aggregate of all active funds, before fees, roughly matches the market by definition (Sharpe, 1991)
- Past performance is not a reliable predictor of future performance

**Hedge funds fare no better.** Kat and Palaro (2006) found only 18% of nearly 2,000 hedge funds outperformed their benchmarks. The standard "two and twenty" fee structure (2% of assets + 20% of gains) consumes most returns. Survivorship bias (failed funds disappear from databases) makes even these poor results look better than reality (Malkiel & Saha, 2005).

**The probability illusion:** With ~8,000 mutual funds, ~2,000 will beat the market in any given year by chance alone. Of those, ~500 will beat it again, and ~125 a third year. This creates the illusion of consistently skilled managers when the pattern is largely random.

### The Psychology of Poor Investment Decisions

Five categories of bias affect investors:

#### 1. Overconfidence Produces Excessive Trading

Overconfidence in one's ability to predict market direction leads to excessive trading. Barber and Odean (2000) studied 66,465 households:
- Average portfolio turnover was 75% annually
- The 20% of accounts with highest turnover earned returns of 16.4% during a booming market -- vs. 17.9% for the overall market
- Highest-turnover investors lost 6.5 percentage points relative to the market

**Gender differences (Barber & Odean, 2001):** Examining 35,000 accounts, women achieved better returns than men -- not because they picked better stocks, but because they traded less. Male turnover averaged 77% annually vs. 53% for women. The added transaction costs from men's more frequent trades (driven by greater overconfidence) wiped out returns.

#### 2. Optimism about Investment Decisions

Moore, Kurtzberg, Fox, and Bazerman (1999) created an investment simulation using 10 real funds over 10 years:
- Starting with $100,000, the optimal strategy (all in index fund) would have grown to $380,041
- The average participant ended with $349,620 due to choosing too many active funds with high fees
- Participants consistently predicted their portfolios would grow faster than they actually did (predicted 8.13% per half-year vs. actual 5.50%)
- At the end, participants believed they had matched the market -- they had actually underperformed by 8%
- They overstated their performance by one entire level on a 7-point scale (Goetzmann & Peles, 1997 found similar results)

Most investors never compare their returns to market benchmarks, protecting their optimistic illusions.

#### 3. Denying that Random Events are Random

Investors see patterns in randomness, treating "hot" funds as skillful rather than lucky. This is the same gamblers-fallacy that creates belief in the "hot hand" in basketball.

**Regression to the mean in investing:** Bogle (1994), Carhart (1997), DeBondt and Thaler (1992) all found fund performance regresses toward the mean. Study participants expected "hot" funds to stay hot -- their expectations were actually *negatively* correlated with actual returns.

**DeBondt and Thaler (1985):** "Loser" portfolios (extreme losers from the past 3 years) dramatically outperformed "winner" portfolios over the following 5 years, because investors overbuy past winners and oversell past losers.

#### 4. Anchoring, the Status Quo, and Procrastination

- **Naive diversification:** Benartzi and Thaler (2001) found professors allocated retirement funds roughly 50:50 between TIAA (bonds) and CREF (stock), never adjusting. When firms offered 4 funds (3 stock, 1 bond), employees put 75% in stock. One stock fund + three bond funds? 75% in bonds. People diversify across *categories offered* like picking one dish from each column in a Chinese restaurant.
- **Status quo bias:** Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988) found that when told they *inherited* an investment, participants overwhelmingly kept it rather than switching to a better-suited option
- **Procrastination:** Automatic enrollment in 401(k) plans increased initial participation from 49% to 86% (Madrian & Shea, 2001). People know they should invest but procrastinate on allocation decisions while paradoxically being overactive in trading within categories.

#### 5. Prospect Theory, Selling Winners, and Keeping Losers

**The disposition effect (Odean, 1998):** Investors have a strong preference to hold stocks below purchase price (avoiding "becoming losers") and sell stocks above purchase price ("becoming winners").

The reference point is the initial purchase price. From prospect-theory:
- Stocks above purchase price = gains domain = risk averse = sell to lock in the sure gain
- Stocks below purchase price = loss domain = risk seeking = hold, hoping for recovery

This is irrational for three reasons:
1. High transaction costs from frequent selling
2. Winners that are sold tend to outperform losers that are kept (Odean, 1999)
3. Tax disadvantage: selling winners creates capital gains tax; selling losers creates tax benefits

Calvet, Campbell, and Sodini (2009): investors become MORE eager to sell winners as performance improves -- the bias intensifies with success.

### Active Trading / Daytrading

Online trading costs fell 75% between 1996-1998, enabling a wave of daytrading. Jordan and Diltz (2003) studied 324 daytraders during the 1998-1999 bubble: only 36% made money, and nearly all profits were short-term capital gains taxed at up to 35%.

Key insight: "When a daytrader is buying a stock, it is because someone else has sold it." The counterparty is typically an institutional investor with better information, more experience, and faster hardware. Daytrading is systematically disadvantageous.

### Action Steps

1. **Determine investment goals** -- define what you need and when you need it
2. **Maximize tax-advantaged savings** -- always contribute enough to get full employer match
3. **Formulate an asset allocation plan** -- long-term investors should weight stocks more heavily (Benartzi & Thaler, 2001)
4. **Invest in low-cost index funds** -- avoid loads, minimize expense ratios
5. **Invest regularly** -- consistent contributions, then ignore the market
6. **Stop paying attention** -- "there is little reason to be thinking about your investments more than a few hours per year"

### Why the Market is Hard to Predict

Keynes's beauty contest analogy: investing is not about picking the best stocks but about predicting what other investors will think are the best stocks -- a recursive problem with no stable solution.

## New Concepts Introduced
- behavioral-finance
- disposition-effect

## Existing Concepts Updated
- overconfidence-in-calibration -- drives excessive trading; gender differences in trading frequency trace to overconfidence gap
- prospect-theory -- directly explains the disposition effect (selling winners, holding losers)
- loss-aversion -- investors avoid "booking" losses by holding declining stocks
- anchoring-and-adjustment -- purchase price anchors investment decisions; listing prices anchor fund selection
- regression-to-the-mean -- investors fail to expect mean reversion in fund performance
- gamblers-fallacy -- "hot fund" thinking mirrors "hot hand" fallacy

## Quotes Worth Keeping
> "The folks who run mutual funds have always been good at cooking up clever ways to gouge you on fees, confuse you about performance, make you pay unnecessary taxes and goad you into buying funds you don't need." -- Jason Zweig, 2000
> "When a daytrader is buying a stock, it is because someone else has sold it. Similarly, when a daytrader sells a stock, someone else is buying it. Odds are that the other party is an institutional investor of some sort." -- Bazerman & Moore

skills.title: Hot-Cold Empathy Gap
skills.subtitle: Calm-you can't predict what angry-you will do
skills.challenge: This week, make one important decision only when you're in a neutral emotional state. If you notice you're hungry, angry, tired, or excited, write down the decision but wait 24 hours. Compare what you wanted to do 'hot' vs. 'cold'.
skills.definition: The hot-cold empathy gap is the systematic failure to appreciate how visceral states (hunger, pain, anger, sexual arousal, craving) influence our own preferences and behavior. In a 'cold' state, we cannot accurately predict what we will want or do when in a 'hot' state, and vice versa. This leads to poor planning, broken commitments, and underestimation of temptation's power.
skills.content:
## Definition

The hot-cold empathy gap is the systematic failure to predict how we will think, feel, and behave when in an emotional state different from our current one. When "cold" (calm, rational), we cannot accurately predict our "hot" (emotional, aroused) selves, and vice versa. The term was developed by George Loewenstein in his landmark 1996 paper "Out of Control: Visceral Influences on Behavior" and explored experimentally by Ariely and Loewenstein in a series of studies through the 2000s.

This is not just a small error: people **massively** underestimate how much emotions will transform their preferences, morality, and risk-taking. The gap exists because emotional states alter not just the intensity of desires but their very structure — hot states create qualitatively different preference orderings, not merely amplified versions of cold-state preferences.

## Loewenstein's Research Program

George Loewenstein's work on the empathy gap is part of his broader research program on **visceral factors** — bodily states such as hunger, thirst, sexual arousal, pain, fatigue, and drug cravings that powerfully influence behavior but are systematically neglected in economic models of decision-making.

### The Visceral Factors Framework (1996)

Loewenstein argued that visceral factors share several features that make them uniquely dangerous for decision-making:

1. **They have a disproportionate effect on behavior.** A hungry person does not merely prefer food slightly more — hunger can dominate all other goals and override long-term plans entirely.
2. **People in one visceral state cannot accurately simulate another.** A satiated person cannot recreate the experience of extreme hunger through imagination alone. The gap is not one of information but of *experiential access*.
3. **The gap is bidirectional but asymmetric.** Cold-to-hot prediction is poor; hot-to-cold prediction is also poor but differently so. People in hot states tend to believe their current feelings will last forever (a form of projection-bias), while people in cold states tend to believe they would never behave the way hot-state people do.
4. **The effect is robust to experience.** Even people who have repeatedly cycled through hot and cold states (e.g., recovering addicts, dieters) fail to accurately predict their hot-state behavior when currently cold.

### The Heroin Addict Studies

Loewenstein's research with heroin addicts provided some of the most striking demonstrations of the empathy gap. In studies with opioid-dependent individuals:

- **When not in withdrawal (cold state):** Addicts expressed strong motivation to stay clean, believed they could resist cravings, and underestimated how powerful withdrawal symptoms would be. They rated their future craving intensity at roughly half of what it actually turned out to be.
- **When in withdrawal (hot state):** The same individuals described cravings as overwhelming and all-consuming. They could not imagine ever having felt indifferent to the drug. Their discount rates for drug rewards became extraordinarily steep — they would sacrifice enormous future benefits for immediate relief.
- **Critical finding:** The gap persisted even among experienced addicts who had cycled through withdrawal many times. Experience with the hot state did not improve cold-state predictions. This challenges the intuition that "I know what it's like, so I can plan for it."

This has profound implications for addiction treatment: relapse prevention plans made during sobriety (cold state) systematically underestimate the pull of cravings (hot state), which is why environmental controls and precommitment devices are more effective than willpower-based strategies.

## The Sexual Arousal Experiment (Ariely Ch. 6)

The Berkeley sexual arousal experiment, conducted by Ariely and Loewenstein, is one of the most vivid demonstrations of the empathy gap in the literature. The study was designed to measure how sexual arousal changes preferences, moral boundaries, and risk tolerance.

### Method

Male Berkeley undergraduates participated in two sessions:

- **Cold-state session:** In a non-aroused state, participants answered a series of questions about their sexual preferences, willingness to engage in morally questionable behavior to obtain sex, and willingness to engage in unsafe sex.
- **Hot-state session:** The same participants answered the identical questions while sexually aroused (they self-stimulated while viewing erotic images on a laptop, answering questions on-screen).

The questions fell into three categories:
1. **Sexual preferences** — attraction to activities outside their normal comfort zone (e.g., unusual fetishes, non-standard scenarios)
2. **Moral boundaries** — willingness to engage in ethically questionable actions to obtain sex (e.g., deception, persistence after being told "no," exploitation of intoxication)
3. **Safe sex practices** — willingness to use condoms, likelihood of forgoing protection

### Results

The cold-to-hot shift was dramatic:

- **72% increase** in attraction to unusual sexual activities — things rated "not at all" attractive in cold state were rated moderately attractive in hot state
- **136% increase** in willingness to engage in morally questionable behavior — the single most alarming finding, suggesting arousal does not merely amplify existing preferences but fundamentally alters moral reasoning
- **25% increase** in willingness to forego condoms — a smaller but practically significant shift with real health consequences

### Why This Study Matters

Several features make this study particularly important:

1. **Familiar emotional territory.** These were college-aged men with extensive experience with sexual arousal. Unlike studies of novel emotions, participants had been in the hot state hundreds or thousands of times. Yet they still could not predict their aroused selves. If experience does not close the gap for the most familiar of emotional states, it likely does not close it for less frequent states either.
2. **The moral dimension.** The 136% increase in willingness to cross moral boundaries is the most important finding. It means the empathy gap is not just about preferences (liking unusual things) but about **ethics and self-control**. People in cold states genuinely believe they would never behave unethically; in hot states, those boundaries become negotiable.
3. **Self-knowledge failure.** Participants did not report being surprised by their hot-state answers. In the moment, their responses felt genuine and consistent with who they were. The gap is invisible from both sides — cold-state you cannot imagine hot-state you, and hot-state you cannot imagine why cold-state you was so conservative.

### Ariely's Childbirth Anecdote

Ariely supplements the experimental data with a personal example: his wife Sumi made a firm commitment during pregnancy (cold state) to refuse painkillers during labor. When actual labor arrived (hot state), she begged for the epidural. The anesthesiologist, following her cold-state instructions, initially refused. After Sumi's repeated desperate requests, he administered it.

This illustrates the practical dilemma of the empathy gap: which self's preferences should be honored — the cold-state self who planned or the hot-state self who is experiencing the moment? There is no easy answer, because both selves are "really you."

## The Hunger and Shopping Studies

Research on the hunger-driven empathy gap complements the arousal studies:

- **Read & van Leeuwen (1998):** Office workers choosing snacks for next week (cold state, after lunch) chose healthy options 74% of the time. The same workers choosing for right now (hot state, when hungry) chose healthy options only 30% of the time. The gap: people assume their future self will have the same healthy preferences as their current satiated self.
- **Grocery shopping studies:** Multiple studies confirm that hungry shoppers buy more calories, more snack foods, and more unplanned items. The standard advice "don't shop hungry" is an informal recognition of the empathy gap. But the deeper point is that even knowing this rule, people systematically underestimate *how much* hunger will distort their purchasing.
- **Nisbett & Kanouse (1969):** Overweight and normal-weight shoppers bought more food when shopping before dinner than after. The effect was larger for overweight individuals, suggesting that sensitivity to visceral states may vary across individuals.

## Connection to Projection Bias

The empathy gap is closely related to **projection-bias** (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue, & Rabin, 2003) — the tendency to project current preferences onto future selves. Projection bias is the formal economic model of what the empathy gap describes psychologically:

- A cold person shopping for winter clothes on a hot day underbuys warm clothing
- A full person grocery shopping underbuys food
- A healthy person making advance directives underestimates how much they will value life extension when actually ill
- A calm person setting up a gym schedule overestimates future motivation

Projection bias predicts that people will systematically make errors in intertemporal choice because they use current utility as an anchor for future utility, with insufficient adjustment. The formal model: predicted future utility = (1-alpha) * actual future utility + alpha * current utility, where alpha represents the degree of projection bias (alpha = 0 is perfectly rational; alpha = 1 is complete projection of current state).

## Mechanisms

1. **State-dependent preferences:** Our preferences are not fixed traits but emergent properties of our current emotional state. Different states activate different neural circuits and produce genuinely different people. This is not metaphorical — fMRI studies show that hot states recruit limbic and reward circuits that are largely dormant during cold states, producing qualitatively different decision processes.
2. **Projection bias:** We project our current state onto our future self, assuming we will feel then as we feel now. This is the default heuristic for predicting future preferences, and it systematically fails when states change.
3. **The "agglomeration of multiple selves":** There is no single integrated self. Dr. Jekyll cannot predict or control Mr. Hyde because they are, functionally, different people. Ariely uses this framing to argue that traditional models of utility maximization by a unified agent are fundamentally flawed.
4. **Asymmetric access:** When calm, we have no experiential access to our passionate selves; when passionate, we have no access to our rational planning selves. Memory of past hot states is itself "cold" — we remember the facts of what we did but not the felt urgency that drove the behavior.
5. **The empathy gap with others:** The same mechanism that prevents us from predicting our own hot states prevents us from understanding others' hot states. Doctors underestimate patients' pain. Judges give harsher sentences before lunch. Policy makers designing drug policy in comfortable offices cannot simulate the experience of addiction.

## Clinical and Practical Applications

### Safe Sex Education
"Just say no" is cold-state advice for hot-state situations — it assumes the aroused teenager will have the same moral clarity as the classroom teenager. The empathy gap research suggests a fundamentally different approach:
- Ensure condoms are always physically available (reduce friction in hot state)
- Teach **avoidance of tempting situations** rather than resistance within them (don't rely on hot-state willpower)
- Use precommitment devices: decisions made in cold states that constrain hot-state options

### Addiction and Relapse Prevention
- People in recovery (cold state) underestimate the power of cravings (hot state). Plans made during sobriety are systematically overconfident.
- Environmental controls must be designed for the worst case: avoid trigger locations, remove substances from the home, establish automatic check-in protocols
- If/when-then plans established during cold states can provide automatic behavioral responses when hot-state cravings arise

### Teenage Driving Safety
Build precautionary devices into cars that operate automatically (speed limits, parental alerts) configured during cold states. Do not rely on teenagers exercising good judgment during the emotional arousal of driving with peers.

### Financial Decisions
- Don't go shopping when emotionally aroused (angry, sad, celebratory)
- Use precommitment devices (automatic savings, credit card limits, cooling-off periods for large purchases) set up during cold states
- The self-control credit card concept (procrastination-and-precommitment) addresses this directly

### Negotiation (Phase 5)
Recognize that anger, excitement, or time pressure during negotiation changes your preferences. Plan walkaway points and commitments in advance during cold states. Write down your batna and minimum acceptable terms before entering the room, because hot-state you may accept deals that cold-state you would reject.

### Diet and Exercise
Commit during cold states (sign up for classes, remove junk food from house, prepare healthy meals in advance) because hot-state willpower is insufficient. Reward substitution — pairing unpleasant behaviors with immediate pleasures — can bridge the gap.

### Medical Decision-Making
Advance directives, pain management choices, and end-of-life decisions are all profoundly affected by the empathy gap. Healthy patients making advance directives (cold state) may choose to refuse life-sustaining treatment, but when actually facing death (hot state), they often want every available intervention. This creates an ethical dilemma with no clean resolution.

## Cross-References
- **Related concepts:** procrastination-and-precommitment, self-control, dual-process-theory, affect-heuristic, visceral-factors, projection-bias, hyperbolic-discounting, want-should-conflict
- **Key authors:** ariely, George Loewenstein
- **Appears in:** summary-2-S1-ariely-ch6, summary-2-S1-ariely-ch7
- **Phase 5 connections:** batna (set walkaway points in cold state), separate-people-from-problem (emotions during negotiation create empathy gaps)
- **Phase 6 connections:** pre-suasion (environmental cues can trigger hot states that alter decisions)

## Open Questions
- Can training or simulation of hot states during cold-state planning improve prediction accuracy? Early evidence from "empathy suits" (simulating elderly mobility limitations) suggests modest improvement, but the gains may not transfer to emotional hot states.
- Does the empathy gap operate symmetrically (hot predicting cold as poorly as cold predicting hot)? Loewenstein's work suggests it is asymmetric, but the precise dynamics remain understudied.
- How do individual differences in emotional reactivity (trait affect intensity, alexithymia, interoceptive sensitivity) modulate the gap?
- What role does mindfulness practice play? If mindfulness improves interoceptive awareness, does it also improve hot-state prediction accuracy?
- Can technology (biometric feedback, real-time emotional state tracking) serve as an external correction mechanism — alerting people when they are in a hot state and their decisions may not reflect their cold-state values?

relatedSummaries.title: Predictably Irrational Ch.6: The Influence of Arousal — Summary
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Dan Ariely
**Type:** Book chapter
**Phase:** 2
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways
1. People in a "cold" (unaroused) state systematically **fail to predict** how they will behave in a "hot" (aroused) emotional state -- the **hot-cold-empathy-gap**
2. The magnitude of this underprediction is massive: arousal increased predicted attraction to unusual sexual activities by ~72%, immoral behavior propensity by ~136%, and unsafe sex likelihood by ~25%
3. We are not one integrated self but more like an "agglomeration of multiple selves" -- Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
4. Emotional states transform decision-making so completely that cold-state commitments may be useless during hot states

## Detailed Notes

### The Berkeley Sexual Arousal Experiment (Ariely & George Loewenstein)
25 male Berkeley undergraduates participated in a two-session study:

**Session 1 (Cold state):** Students answered questions while calm and unaroused, predicting what they would find attractive, whether they would engage in immoral acts, and whether they would use condoms -- all hypothetically during arousal.

**Session 2 (Hot state):** Same students answered the same questions while actually sexually aroused (viewing erotic images and masturbating, with a Saran-wrapped laptop).

### Results Across Three Categories
**Sexual preferences (19 questions):** Aroused predictions were nearly **twice as high** (72% higher) as cold-state predictions. Activities considered unappealing when cold became much more appealing when aroused.

**Immoral behavior (5 questions):** Propensity to engage in immoral activities was **more than twice as high** (136% higher) when aroused. For example:
- "Would you keep trying after your date says no?" -- Cold: 20, Aroused: 45 (125% increase)
- "Would you slip a woman a drug?" -- Cold: 5, Aroused: 26 (420% increase)

**Unsafe sex (3 questions):** When aroused, participants were 25% more likely to predict foregoing condoms, despite years of safe-sex education.

### The Jekyll and Hyde Insight
- Even the most brilliant, rational person, in the heat of passion, becomes "absolutely and completely divorced from the person he thought he was"
- It is not just that people make wrong predictions about themselves -- **their predictions are wrong by a large margin**
- Our inability to understand ourselves in a different emotional state does **not improve with experience** -- Berkeley students spent substantial time in aroused states yet still couldn't predict their aroused selves

### Practical Implications
- **Safe sex:** "Just say no" campaigns assume we can turn off passion at will. The research shows this is false. Better strategy: ensure condoms are always available (don't decide in a cold state whether to carry one), and teach strategies for avoiding situations where arousal takes over
- **Safe driving:** A teenager driving alone is 40% more likely to crash than an adult; with one friend, risk doubles; with a third teenager, it doubles again. Cars should have built-in precautionary devices (speed limits, parental alerts) configured during cold states
- **Better life decisions:** A cold-state commitment to refuse painkillers during childbirth may evaporate during actual labor. The gap between predicted and experienced emotion must be bridged through advance planning
- **General principle:** Avoid temptation rather than trying to overcome it. Fighting temptation after it arises is much harder than avoiding it in the first place

### Connection to Chapter 7
The inability to predict our hot-state behavior connects directly to procrastination: we make cool, rational plans but then succumb to hot-state impulses (the dessert cart, the new purchase, the skipped exercise session). Understanding the hot-cold gap is essential for designing commitment devices.

## New Concepts Introduced
- hot-cold-empathy-gap -- inability to predict behavior in emotional states different from the current one

## Cross-References
- **Related concepts:** dual-process-theory, self-control, affect-heuristic, visceral-factors
- **Key authors:** ariely, George Loewenstein
- **Connections:** Loewenstein's broader research on visceral factors in decision-making

## Quotes Worth Keeping
> "Even the most brilliant and rational person, in the heat of passion, seems to be absolutely and completely divorced from the person he thought he was." -- Ariely, Ch.6

> "We all systematically underpredict the degree to which arousal completely negates our superego, and the way emotions can take control of our behavior." -- Ariely, Ch.6

skills.definition: Escalation of commitment is the tendency for decision-makers to continue and increase investment in a previously selected course of action beyond what rational analysis would prescribe, particularly after receiving negative feedback. It is the behavioral manifestation of the sunk cost fallacy, driven by self-justification, loss aversion, and impression management.
skills.content:
## Definition

Escalation of commitment is the tendency for decision-makers to continue -- and increase -- investment in a previously selected course of action beyond what rational analysis would prescribe, particularly after receiving negative feedback about the initial decision. It is the behavioral manifestation of the sunk-cost-fallacy, driven by self-justification, loss-aversion, impression management, and competitive dynamics.

## Key Findings

- **Staw (1976) R&D allocation experiment:** Participants who made the initial investment (high-responsibility) allocated significantly more funds to a failing division than those told someone else made the initial decision (low-responsibility). When the initial investment succeeded, allocations were equal. **The mechanism is self-justification** -- negative feedback is dissonant with the initial decision, and further investment resolves the dissonance. (summary-2-08-bazerman-ch8)
- **Staw and Ross (1978):** Escalation is more pronounced when failure can be attributed to external causes (economic downturn) rather than the decision itself
- **Bazerman, Giuliano, & Appelman (1984):** Groups are less likely to escalate than individuals, but groups that escalate do so to a greater degree
- **Schoorman (1988):** Supervisors who participated in hiring decisions positively biased subsequent performance appraisals. Those who disagreed with the hire biased appraisals negatively.
- **Staw & Hoang (1995):** NBA teams gave more playing time and were less likely to trade higher draft picks regardless of actual performance -- sunk cost of draft position influenced playing decisions
- **Friedman (1996):** Mountain climbers escalate commitment in life-or-death conditions. Jeffrey Z. Rubin, escalation scholar, died in a 1995 climbing accident.
- **Nick Leeson / Barings Bank (1995):** Classic escalation -- hid early trading losses, escalated to ever-larger gambles in the loss domain, destroyed a 233-year-old bank ($1.4B losses)

## Mechanisms

Four additive causes:

**1. Perceptual biases:** Confirmation bias leads decision-makers to selectively attend to information supporting the initial decision and ignore disconfirming evidence (Staw, 1980; Caldwell & O'Reilly, 1982).

**2. Judgmental biases:** loss-aversion and framing-effects. Quitting is framed as accepting a sure loss. Continuing is a gamble that might recover. Risk seeking in the loss domain (from prospect-theory) drives continued investment.

**3. Impression management:** Admitting failure is costly to reputation. Society rewards consistency and punishes "flip-flopping" (Staw & Ross, 1980). Ross and Staw (1986): people are more likely to be rewarded for escalating than for changing course.

**4. Competitive irrationality** (specific to competitive escalation): The desire to "win" replaces the goal of profit. See competitive-escalation.

## Applications

- **Management:** Separate initial decision-makers from subsequent evaluators. Reward decision quality at each stage, not consistency (Staw & Ross, 1987). Hedge funds rotate portfolios so the trader who bought does not also decide when to sell.
- **Personal decisions:** Recognize when "I've invested too much to quit" is sunk-cost reasoning. Evaluate only future costs and benefits.
- **Investing:** Set stop-loss orders in advance, before emotional attachment develops
- **Negotiation (Phase 5):** Be aware that your counterpart may be escalating due to prior investment, making them less flexible. Also watch for your own escalation.
- **Pre-mortem exercise:** Ku (2008) -- imagining regret from escalation BEFORE entering a situation reduces subsequent escalation

## Cross-References
- **Related concepts:** sunk-cost-fallacy, competitive-escalation, commitment-and-consistency, cognitive-dissonance, loss-aversion, framing-effects
- **Source:** summary-2-08-bazerman-ch8
- **Key researchers:** Barry Staw, Jerry Ross, Bazerman

## Open Questions
- Can organizations design decision architectures that systematically prevent escalation without also preventing valuable persistence?
- How does escalation interact with culture? Do collectivistic cultures (where face is more important) show more impression-management-driven escalation?
- Is there an optimal point at which persistence becomes escalation, or is it always context-dependent?

relatedSummaries.title: Judgment in Managerial Decision Making Ch.8 — The Escalation of Commitment
relatedSummaries.authors: Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
relatedSummaries.content:
**Author(s):** Max H. Bazerman, Don A. Moore
**Type:** Book chapter (8th Ed, Ch.8, pp.119-131)
**Phase:** 2
**Date ingested:** 2026-04-14

## Key Takeaways

1. Escalation of commitment is the degree to which an individual continues a previously selected course of action beyond what rational analysis would prescribe -- driven by sunk costs, self-justification, and impression management
2. The unilateral escalation paradigm shows that personal responsibility for the initial decision significantly increases subsequent escalation (Staw, 1976)
3. Competitive escalation (the dollar auction) produces systematically irrational outcomes where both parties lose, as the motive shifts from profit-seeking to "winning"
4. Four additive causes drive escalation: perceptual biases (confirmation), judgmental biases (loss framing), impression management (saving face/appearing consistent), and competitive irrationality
5. Organizations can reduce escalation by separating initial decision-makers from subsequent evaluators, rewarding decision quality over outcomes, and rotating responsibilities

## Detailed Notes

### The Core Problem
Three opening scenarios illustrate universal escalation situations:
1. Hiring a manager who underperforms -- should you fire her or invest more?
2. Staying at a disappointing job because of benefits and years invested
3. A startup needing $1M more after you invested $2M -- "good news is we can fix it with more money"

Common element: a prior decision, significant investment, and things not going as planned. The key is distinguishing rational persistence from nonrational escalation.

### Sunk Costs
Accountants and economists agree: sunk costs are historical, irrecoverable, and should not influence future decisions. The reference point should be the current state, evaluating only future costs and benefits. Example: whether to quit a doctoral program -- irrelevant whether it took 6 months or 4 years to reach this point.

Yet typical training in sunk costs "seldom translates to wise solutions to real-world problems" because it lacks description of WHY we intuitively include sunk costs.

### The Unilateral Escalation Paradigm
**Staw (1976) landmark experiment:**
- High-responsibility group: Made an initial R&D allocation to one of two divisions, then learned it failed, then made a second allocation
- Low-responsibility group: Told another officer made the initial decision, then made the second allocation
- **Result:** When the initial investment failed, high-responsibility participants allocated significantly more to the same failing division than low-responsibility participants did
- When the initial decision succeeded, allocation amounts were roughly equal across groups
- **Conclusion:** The mechanism is self-justification. Negative feedback creates dissonance with the initial decision, and escalation resolves it by "proving" the initial choice will eventually succeed.

**Additional findings on escalation:**
- Staw and Ross (1978): Escalation increases when failure can be attributed to external causes (economy, not poor judgment)
- Bazerman, Giuliano, and Appelman (1984): Groups are less likely to escalate than individuals, but groups that DO escalate do so to a greater degree
- Schoorman (1988): Supervisors who participated in a hiring decision positively biased subsequent performance appraisals of that employee
- Staw and Hoang (1995): NBA teams gave more playing time to higher draft picks regardless of actual performance, and higher picks were less likely to be traded

**Friedman (1996):** Mountain climbers' escalation in life-or-death decisions. Jeffrey Z. Rubin, a noted escalation scholar, died in a 1995 climbing accident. His partner had turned back earlier, believing conditions too dangerous.

### Organizational remedies for unilateral escalation:
- Separate initial decision-makers from subsequent evaluators
- Hedge fund portfolio rotation: different traders buy and sell
- Be cognizant of the natural tendency to escalate after negative feedback

### The Competitive Escalation Paradigm
**The $20 bill auction (Shubik, 1971):**
- Auctioneer sells a $20 bill. Highest bidder wins, but the SECOND-highest bidder also pays their bid and gets nothing.
- Bidding starts fast, slows at $12-$16 as most drop out, leaving two trapped bidders
- The $16 bidder must bid $18 or accept a $16 loss. The uncertain gamble of continuing always looks better than the certain loss of quitting.
- This continues past $20. "The decision to bid $21 is very similar to all previous decisions"
- Bidding typically ends $20-$70, has hit $100. Authors have earned over $30,000 running this in 20 years of classes.
- **Key insight:** The problem is entering the auction. Once in, each incremental bid looks rational. The trap must be identified before entry.

**Corporate escalation -- companies A, B, C:**
Company C (worth $1B standalone, $1.2B if acquired) creates escalation between A and B. If A acquires C, B loses $0.5B in competitive position. This triggers bidding spirals where the acquisition price exceeds standalone value.

**Real-world corporate escalation cases:**
- 1995 USAir: American Airlines avoided escalation through Crandall's open letter signaling mutual destruction
- 2004-2006 Guidant acquisition: J&J and Boston Scientific engaged in classic escalation despite mounting evidence of Guidant's product defects (defibrillator recall). Boston Scientific ultimately paid $27B -- more than J&J's original $25.4B pre-scandal bid. Boston Scientific's stock fell from $35.88 to below $17.
- Reverse-bid auctions in procurement produce the same escalation in the opposite direction

### Why Does Escalation Occur? Four Causes

**1. Perceptual Biases:**
- Confirmation bias (Staw, 1980): After committing to a course of action, decision-makers selectively attend to confirming information
- Caldwell and O'Reilly (1982): People who freely choose a course of action selectively filter information to maintain commitment
- **Remedy:** Search for disconfirming information. Use objective outsiders. Imagine future regret before entering (Ku, 2008 -- reduces escalation in subsequent auctions)

**2. Judgmental Biases:**
- Losses from initial investment frame continuation as a choice between a sure loss (quitting) and a gamble (continuing might recover)
- loss-aversion and risk seeking in losses drive continued investment
- Nick Leeson / Barings Bank (1995): Leeson hid early trading losses, escalated to ever-larger gambles in the loss domain, and ultimately caused the collapse of the 233-year-old bank ($1.4B in losses)
- **Remedy:** A different decision-maker evaluating from a different reference point would be less likely to continue

**3. Impression Management:**
- Admitting failure (firing the employee you hired) is a public acknowledgment of error
- Staw and Ross (1980): Society perceives consistent leaders as better than those who change course
- Kerry vs. Bush 2004: Kerry's "I voted for it before I voted against it" was used as evidence of indecisiveness. Bush's unwavering positions were lauded as strength of character despite unpopularity.
- Ross and Staw (1986): People are more likely to be rewarded for escalating than for changing course
- **Remedy:** Replace systems that reward impression management. Reward decision quality at each stage (Staw & Ross, 1987), not consistency. Evaluate the process, not just the outcome.

**4. Competitive Irrationality:**
- Unique to the competitive paradigm: the desire to "win" replaces the goal of profit
- Ku, Malhotra, & Murnighan (2005): Art auction bidders bid more than they valued the art
- Ku, Galinsky, & Murnighan (2006): Online auctions with many bidders drive prices above cheaper alternatives
- **Remedy:** Consider the other party's perspective. Recognize that opportunities often prove to be traps.

### Integration
Four additive causes work together. Managers should:
- Take an experimental approach to management: implement, but be ready to drop commitment if it fails
- Constantly reassess the rationality of future commitments
- Focus on future costs and benefits, disregarding sunk costs
- Balance caution about escalation with the value of maintaining commitments that preserve future options

## New Concepts Introduced
- escalation-of-commitment
- sunk-cost-fallacy
- competitive-escalation

## Existing Concepts Updated
- commitment-and-consistency -- dark side: consistency pressure drives irrational escalation
- cognitive-dissonance -- self-justification as the core mechanism of unilateral escalation (Staw, 1976)
- loss-aversion -- risk seeking in losses drives continued investment in failing courses of action
- framing-effects -- loss framing of sunk costs makes quitting feel like accepting a sure loss

## Quotes Worth Keeping
> "If at first you don't succeed, try, try, again. Then quit. No use being a damn fool about it." -- W. C. Fields (chapter epigraph)
> "You may not always agree with me, but you know what I stand for." -- George W. Bush, 2004 (on the value society places on consistency)

relatedSummaries.title: Conflict Resolution: A Cognitive Perspective — Summary
relatedSummaries.source: 2-07 - Choices, Values, and Frames (Collection) - Kahneman, Tversky
relatedSummaries.content:
## Key Takeaways

- Three cognitive phenomena — **optimistic overconfidence**, the **certainty effect**, and **loss-aversion** — create systematic barriers to successful negotiation and conflict resolution
- These biases are departures from rational judgment; if people behaved according to the standard rational model, these barriers would be reduced or eliminated
- **Concession aversion** (a novel concept introduced here) means each side evaluates its own concessions as losses and the opponent's concessions as gains, shrinking the perceived zone of possible agreement
- The **certainty effect** causes negotiators to underweight uncertain benefits of agreement (e.g., future goodwill) relative to certain or contingently certain outcomes, reducing the perceived value of deals
- **Fairness judgments** are reference-dependent and self-serving — disputants often agree on fairness principles but disagree on the reference point, creating pseudo-fairness deadlocks
- Understanding these biases operates on two levels: (1) recognizing the opponent's irrationality, and (2) recognizing one's own susceptibility to the same biases

## Detailed Notes

### I. Optimistic Overconfidence

Kahneman and Tversky identify two interacting phenomena that fuel overconfidence in conflict:

**Overconfidence in judgment.** People assign probabilities that are more extreme than their knowledge warrants. Confidence intervals are systematically too narrow. When given one-sided evidence, subjects are *more* confident in their predictions than those given both sides, despite being less accurate (Brenner, Koehler, and Tversky 1992).
